paragraphs.text: BOOK ONE.

Gaudentius, Donatist bishop of Thamugadi, was threatening to burn himself in his church together with some lost souls who had joined him. The eminent Dulcitius, tribune and notary, had been charged by our most pious emperor with carrying out his laws in order to bring about unity. Dealing gently with these raging men, as was right, he first sent Gaudentius a peaceable letter. Gaudentius wrote back two letters. One was shorter and, as he says, hurried because its carriers were in a hurry. The other was longer, and in it he believes he has answered more carefully, according to the scriptures. With the Lord's help, then, I have undertaken to refute his writings in such a way that even the slower-witted will not doubt that I have answered every point. I will first set down his words and then add ours, but not in the way I did when I answered the letters of Petilian. There, at each point where his words were inserted, I wrote "Petilian said," and where my words were given, "Augustine replied." For this he slandered me as though I had lied, saying that he had never disputed with me face to face. As if he did not say what he wrote because I did not hear it from his lips but read it in his letters! Or as if I did not answer him because I did not speak in his presence, but replied to his writings by writing in turn! What are we to do with people who have such a heart, or who suppose that those they want to read their writings have such a heart? Still, let us satisfy even such people here. When we set down the words of Gaudentius, let us not say "Gaudentius said" but "Words of the letter"; and when we answer, let us not say "Augustine replied" but "Reply." So let us begin by refuting the first and shorter letter of Gaudentius.

Words of the letter: "To the honorable Dulcitius, tribune and notary, much longed for by us, if you will have it so, Gaudentius the bishop." Reply: We ought not to discuss even this, or we shall almost be dwelling on trifles, when there are essential passages that will compel us to speak at somewhat greater length.

Words of the letter: "I have received the letter of Your Piety through men who, it is plain, are dear to all for their character and their way of life." Reply: Nor will I discuss how you could say "Your Piety" to a man you consider impious instead. You returned the courtesy as you thought it ought to be returned. After all, he treated you more courteously in the letter he sent you than a Catholic ought to treat a heretic, because he thought such language might make your mind curable.

Words of the letter: "In it," he says, "Your Worthiness said a great many things about which I keep silent for the present. But the sharpness of your mind failed to notice that in that same letter you could declare us neither fully innocent nor guilty." Reply: How did he not declare them guilty when he said they had been wrongly gathered together? How did he not declare you guilty when he said that under your leadership the souls of the wretched would perish by an unspeakable death? He added that you ought to understand what odium might await you in this world, and what punishment at that last judgment, where there is no hope. How did he not declare you guilty when he urged you as best he could to follow the example of others who deserve to be imitated, to abandon the error of your former heresy, and to come over to the one true faith of God? But we have undertaken to refute the words of the heretic, not to defend the words of the tribune. So if this man of ours, being a layman and a soldier, said something rather carelessly, who would not pardon him? Who would argue that his words should prejudice the case of the Catholic Church? You, however, should consider more carefully what you say, since at our conference held at Carthage the party of Donatus put you forward, along with six others, as a defender of its schism.

Words of the letter: "But if you consider us criminals," he says, "you must flee our society as deserving condemnation." Reply: Certainly the society of criminals must be fled, but the society of the corrected must not be rejected. So we avoid the first for the sake of salvation, but in such a way that we mercifully desire, long for, and press for the second.

Words of the letter: "But if you consider us innocent," he says, "as you yourself have said, then we who stand firm in the faith of Christ rejoice to endure persecutors." Reply: I have looked over the tribune's letter to you, and nowhere in it did I read that he called you innocent. He said that he had heard or learned from others that you were prudent. In the holy scriptures, however, not only the good but also the wicked are commonly called prudent. Indeed, the serpent who deceived man received this name there. Where some have translated "the wisest of all the beasts," the Greek manuscripts from which that scripture was translated into Latin have "the most prudent" instead. But suppose we must think that the tribune called innocent those whom he said you were holding against their will for destruction. Is it any wonder that he believed this was happening there too, since he knew it had happened in other places? So you have no reason to rejoice that you suffer persecution, since you can find no way to show that you are innocent. Far be it from us to call this a persecution of men. It is rather a persecution of vices, for the sake of setting men free, such as the diligence of physicians also carries out on the sick. And yet even if you were innocent, this would make you guilty, because you want to kill innocent people. For when people try to show that they are innocent and yet refuse to spare their own lives, what are they convicted of but killing the innocent?

Words of the letter: "But in this church," he says, "in which the name of God and of his Christ has always been continually invoked in truth, as you yourself said, we will either remain alive as long as it pleases God, or, as befits the household of God, we will end our lives within the Lord's camp. This is on one condition, namely, that it may happen if force is used. For no one is so mad as to hasten to death when no one is driving him." Reply: Nor do we read in the tribune's letter that the name of God was invoked by you in truth, although he did say "invoked." And even if he had said it, it could be understood as pointing not to your glory but to your punishment. For the apostle said of the ungodly Gentiles that they "hold the truth in iniquity." That is what you do, for you hold the truth of divine baptism in the iniquity of human error. So when we correct your iniquity, we certainly must not undo the truth of that sacrament. You profess openly, innocent man, though in other words, that you and your people will perish together with the church. For when you say "in the church," what else do you want us to understand but "with the church," since you are preparing to do it with fire? This is the innocence of the party of Donatus! You plan to do this, adding your own deaths, to the very thing you are charged with having done at Carthage without your deaths, in order to bring odium on us. There you did it to the basilicas that had been yours, as far as you could and with whatever helpers you could find. For who would not believe that you did that out of zeal, when you are planning to do the same thing even at the cost of your lives? And if you did not do that, then what you are now preparing to do is certainly more insane. But you said, "if force is used," and added, "for no one is so mad as to hasten to death when no one is driving him." How much madder, then, is the man who hastens to death when he is being driven toward life!

Words of the letter: "As for those who are with us," he says, "I call God and all his sacraments to witness that I have exhorted them, and urged them most earnestly, that anyone who wished to leave should say so publicly and without fear. For we cannot hold back the unwilling, since we have learned that no one is to be compelled to the faith of God." Reply: Even if you do not hold anyone back against their will, why do you not openly profess yourself to be one who urges them to a good work, if what you are about to do is good? Or perhaps you yourself understand how evil it is, and you threaten to do it more to frighten us than to carry it out. If so, then either you are faithless because you are lying, or you are cruel because you are telling the truth.

Words of the letter (and in another hand): "I pray that you may be safe and flourish in the affairs of state, and that you may cease from troubling Christians." Reply: We too can pray that he may be safe and flourish in the affairs of state, but not that he may cease from correcting heretics.

Words of the later letter: "To Dulcitius, honorable and longed for with all affection, Gaudentius the bishop." Reply: If you long for the man with all affection, why do you refuse to hold fast to the unity of Christ with him? Or are you repaying evil for evil, as it were, by wanting to rebaptize the one you think is your persecutor?

Words of the letter: "People who know each other only by reputation," he says, "usually wish either to meet face to face and talk together, or at least, if they are strangers, not to shrink from each other's presence. But Your Judgment has made known by letter that you were glad to find me absent and saddened that I had returned." Reply: Not all who know each other only by reputation wish to see each other, but only those whom that reputation commends well. What has happened to you is truly strange. You say that you long for the man by whom you complain you are suffering persecution, while he who persecutes you would prefer you to be absent, and does not want to find the man he is persecuting. How can this be, unless he wanted it understood that you are rather the persecutor of those whose salvation in Christ he believed your presence would hinder?

Words of the letter: "Yesterday," he says, "so as not to leave you without a written reply, I set out certain points briefly and concisely because the carriers were in a hurry. Now I must answer the letter of Your Worthiness with the words of the most holy divine law. The Lord says: 'You shall not kill the innocent and the righteous, and you shall not clear the guilty.' It is certain, therefore, that in God's judgment the one who acquits the guilty and the one who kills the innocent are bound by equal crime and equal guilt. If Gabinius, whom you named, or the other breakers of faith who shared in that evil lapse were guilty before they entered your communion, then according to God's words they should by no means have been acquitted. But if they were received as innocent or holy, why do you kill the innocent who remain in the same faith from which you accept those men as saints?" Reply: What you say is spiteful and false. The man you are addressing has not received an order that you be killed, but that you be corrected. If you refuse, you will be sent into exile, so that you may not hinder the correction of others. If the just ought not to do this to the unjust, why did you wish, falsely besides, to boast at our conference about Caecilian's exile? You claimed that the emperor Constantine sent him into it at the urging of your forebears. But this tribune to whom you are writing, who has been given charge of the laws enacted for the sake of unity, wants you to live so much that he fears you may kill yourself. Look, set him and yourself before your eyes! He wants you to live in the peace of Christ; you seek to kill yourself in the party of Donatus. Recognize which of you is your persecutor.

Gabinius, who is now ours but was once yours, and a great many others have come over from you to us after considering the Catholic truth. You should not think that they have not been cleansed from your contagion simply because we did not rebaptize them. Those who have not yet been baptized are washed from all their sins in the Catholic Church by the bath of regeneration. But there are those who received this sacrament outside the Church, not for their help but for their judgment. We do not violate the royal mark even in a deserter, so in their case what is written comes to pass: "Love covers a multitude of sins." See how those who must not be baptized can be cleansed by the very love of Catholic unity. It is not that something begins to be in them inside the Church which was not in them outside. Rather, what harmed them outside begins to benefit them inside. So we do not receive them from you as saints, for they are sanctified by coming over to us, and while they remained with you they could not be holy at all. Nor do we kill you as innocent; we want you to live even though you are guilty.

You recall the testimony of the divine voice well, and you throw it at us that God said, "You shall not kill the innocent and the righteous." But if you are innocent and righteous, why are you killing yourself? We do not call you innocent and righteous, and yet we do not want you to be killed. You consider yourself innocent and righteous, and yet you do not spare an innocent and righteous man. You yourself said that in God's judgment the one who acquits the guilty and the one who kills the innocent are bound by equal crime and equal guilt. Why then did you acquit Felician the Maximianist, a guilty man? Why are you killing an innocent man, namely yourself? We, on the other hand, do not acquit the guilty; we wish him first to be corrected so that he may deserve to be acquitted. Nor do we judge you innocent if you remain in the party of Donatus, whether you spare yourself or kill yourself. However much you boast of your innocence, you cannot be innocent if you kill yourself as an innocent man. Unless perhaps you answer me and say: "When I kill myself, I am certainly not killing an innocent man, because by the very will with which I resolve to kill myself I become guilty in mind before I kill the body." If you say this, you speak the truth, and you defend yourself in a wonderful way, by accusing yourself. For if you show that in killing yourself you first become guilty by your very intention, then once the deed is done no one will be able to convict you of killing an innocent man. By this reasoning it follows that, although many innocent people are killed by others, no innocent person is killed by himself. For the very thought with which he plans to kill himself first strips him of his innocence, so that when he does kill himself he does not die innocent. This would apply to you if you had been innocent before you prepared to kill yourself. But as it is, you were not innocent even before, since you are a heretic. So if you kill yourself, that will not be the beginning of your wickedness but an increase of it.

Words of the letter: "As for holy Emeritus of Caesarea," he says, "the report that reached us about him was false, as his merit would lead us to expect. But even if it were true, listen to the apostle saying: 'If some of them have fallen away from the faith, has their unbelief made void the faith of God? By no means.'" Reply: We must say about Emeritus of Caesarea what you were afraid to say. A false report was indeed spread about him, that he had become a Catholic. But just as you heard that, you could also have learned everything that actually happened. Why, then, did you choose to say nothing in praise of your fellow bishop, when his name was put before you as an example? Surely, if he did anything praiseworthy at so critical a moment, you would not have kept quiet about it. You do not want us to believe that you could have envied his praise. So why were you silent, unless you were afraid you would have to blush for him? Well then, Emeritus came to Caesarea while we were staying there. He came, not tracked down by anyone's cunning or brought there by anyone's authority, but moved by his own will, because he wanted to see us. We saw him, and we went together to the Catholic church. A very large crowd was there. He could say nothing in defense of himself or of you. He refused to enter communion, persisted when given time, fell silent when refuted, and went away unharmed. What could have been gentler, as befits our mildness? What could have shown the Catholic truth more unconquerable? What could have been more beneficial for your correction, if you had any sense? He would not have come to us of his own accord unless he meant to say something for you against us. So he surely would have said it, if he had found anything to say. Whatever he had prepared to say, which was why he came, was refuted beforehand by us, with the help of the Lord's mercy, before he could bring it forward to trap us. And if you think that he could have answered but would not, read the record of what passed with him and answer it yourself. If Emeritus had come over into Catholic peace, you would say that he had not consented to the light of truth by God's mercy but had given in to the weight of persecution out of human weakness. Again, if he had been arrested and brought against his will, you would boast as you pleased that he kept silent not for lack of an answer but as a way of escaping. As it is, since he came of his own accord, it was surely not his tongue that failed him when he fell silent, but his case. And as for his refusal to come over into Catholic unity, it was his shame that made his proud soul so very stubborn. But this did as much for the strengthening and salvation of others as it did for his own ruin and punishment. For if people had seen Emeritus entering communion with us, they would have suspected that he was afraid. But they saw him remain in the party of Donatus and yet say nothing against the Catholic faith. So it became all the clearer to them that by his silence he was crying out for us against his own side. Standing there with his voice and mouth sound and free, was not that Emeritus a fitting witness for our cause against you? That Emeritus, I say, at once our enemy and mute?

But you thought you had done well to console your people, and with apostolic authority at that. You did not cite the apostle's words on account of Emeritus. He could do no more for you than this: finding nothing to say on your behalf, he still did not leave you. You cited them on account of others, who have abandoned your error and are being joined to the Catholic fellowship, changed for the better. That is why you recalled that the apostle said: "If some of them have fallen away from the faith, has their unbelief made void the faith of God? By no means." Truly, all that is left is to say that those who believed God have fallen away from the faith, while those who believe men hold the faith! The Lord said, "In your seed shall all nations be blessed": see whom they believe who come over from you to us. Men said that the nations overseas perished through the sin of Caecilian: see whom they believe who remain in your fellowship. And you say that those who followed the faith of God have fallen away from the faith, while those who have remained with the words of men have the faith of God! What then becomes of what the apostle added right after the sentence you quoted: "But God is true, and every man a liar"? Can it be that those who believe what the Lord God, who is true, has said have fallen away from the faith, while those who believe what a lying man has said remain in the faith?

Words of the letter: "You urge me to flee," he says, "as if on the basis of the law. But only one who does the law ought to be listened to, since the apostle Paul says: 'It is not the hearers of the law who are righteous before God, but the doers of the law will be justified.' Listen also to the Lord saying that the good shepherd lays down his life for his sheep, but the hireling, who does not own the sheep, sees the wolf coming and flees, and the wolf seizes them and scatters them." Reply: See how the party of Donatus understands the gospel! Was the apostle, then, not a shepherd but a hireling when he was let down over the wall in a basket and fled from the hands of the man who wanted to seize him? And are you a shepherd? You want to destroy along with yourself, and you seek to kill along with yourself, those you call the Lord's sheep, so that they perish in mind through error and destroy their bodies through madness. Do you not hear the Shepherd and Prince of shepherds saying, "The thief comes only to kill and destroy"? Is this why you came, you who had gone away? Is this why you returned, you who had fled? This is the work of a thief and a robber, not of a shepherd and guardian. And yet see, even without our pressing you, that you would not want all your colleagues who fled to be understood as hirelings rather than shepherds. But if the Lord's sheep were with you, they would either come along with you, so that they might have you as their shepherd once you were corrected, or they would leave you and flee to the Shepherd. The hireling the Lord means flees from the wolf, not in body but in mind, when out of fear he abandons righteousness. That is how your Secundus of Tigisis fled when he feared Purpurius of Limata, who had confessed to murder and was all the more terrifying for it, lest he lose his primacy or his bishopric. In body, however, even those good shepherds the apostles fled in persecution, and yet they did not therefore abandon Christ's sheep in their care and concern. If you too were a shepherd, then first of all you would not be on the side of the wolf. Second, you would have obediently heard the command of your Lord, who ordered his servants to flee in times of persecution, through anyone's mouth, even a sinner's. And you would not argue against your Lord and say: "Only one who does the law ought to be listened to, since the apostle Paul says: 'It is not the hearers of the law who are righteous before God, but the doers of the law will be justified.'"

Why do you twist plain words into another meaning? The apostle denied that hearers of the law who are not doers are righteous before God. He did not forbid people to be heard when they speak the truth; otherwise he would have spoken, as you do, against his Lord, who says of certain people: “Do what they tell you, but do not do what they do. For they speak and do not act.” You see how Christ commanded others to hear the law, and to be doers of it, even through men who were hearers and preachers of the law but not its doers. Yet you say, “Only the doer of the law should be heard,” and in your wish to refute your supposed persecutor you speak against your Creator. It is true that the Lord says to the sinner: “Why do you recite my statutes and take my covenant in your mouth?” But he says this because it profits nothing to the one who speaks and does not do what he says. It does profit the one who hears what is good, even through a bad man, and does what he hears. Praise is indeed not fitting in the mouth of a sinner, but it is fitting in the life and conduct of one who does it, even if he heard it from a sinner’s mouth. So think the tribune as great a sinner as you like, and no doer of the law. Still, obediently hear not him but the One who speaks even through him: “If they persecute you in one city, flee to another.” Why do you stand still? Hear and flee. Christ commands this, not the tribune. Unless perhaps you answer: “Christ does say, ‘If they persecute you in this city, flee to another.’ But why should I leave this city, when this man is not my persecutor and I am not a hearer of Christ?” And so, if you stay, you are a raging wolf, and if you flee, you are a frightened wolf. And the Bridegroom says: “If you do not know yourself, O fairest among women, go out in the tracks of the flocks and feed your kids by the tents of the shepherds.” So even if you boast that you are a shepherd, because you have gone out of the Lord’s fold you are feeding your own kids, not Christ’s sheep.

The words of the letter: “Next,” he says, “what places will there be to receive bishops, as into a harbor, and keep them in peace when they are tossed on every side in this storm of persecution? The Lord did say, ‘When they begin to persecute you in this city, flee to another.’ The apostles fled safely back then, because the emperor had ordered no one to be proscribed on their account. But now those who would take in Christians are terrified by proscriptions and dread the dangers. Not only do they refuse to take them in; they are even afraid to see those whom they secretly revere.” To this the reply: I certainly commend you for recognizing what you are, but I grieve that you do not correct yourselves. What could be plainer than this admission of yours? By it you declare clearly enough that you do not belong to the company of those to whom the Lord said: “If they persecute you in one city, flee to another.” This is exactly what I said a little earlier you could answer me with complete truth, if you were to say: “This man is not my persecutor, and I am not a hearer of Christ.” And look, you say it quite openly. For how are you a hearer of Christ? He promises his hearers, that is, his followers, that until the end of the age, whenever they suffer persecution, they will never lack cities to take refuge in. He says: “When they persecute you in this city, flee to another. For truly I tell you, you will not finish going through the cities of Israel before the Son of Man comes.” But you say that in this persecution you complain of suffering, you already lack places to flee to, where you can rest from this storm as if in a harbor. In saying so you speak against the promise of Christ, who says that his own who suffer persecution will not lack cities to flee to until he comes, that is, until the end of the age. He promised his own something that you cannot find. So if you are his, he is certainly a liar; but since he does not lie, you are not his. And so the tribune you are answering is not your persecutor. He is the persecutor of your persecutor, that is, of your error. That error drives you to do such things that you belong to the kind of people of whom it is written that they suffered persecution from their own deeds. So if you understood what it is in you that those who love you are persecuting, you would surely flee your evil deeds, which are the very things persecuting you. And you would join those who persecute your persecutors in order to set you free, for it is only your errors that they persecute.

The words of the letter: “Almighty God,” he says, “fashioned man through the Maker of all things, the Lord Christ, and left him, as one like God, to free choice. For it is written: ‘God made man and left him in the hand of his own choice.’ Why is human authority now snatching from me what God has bestowed? Consider, most eminent sir, what great sacrileges are committed against God when human presumption takes away what he has granted, and vainly boasts that it does so on God’s behalf. It is a great insult to God if he is defended by men. What does someone think of God when he wants to defend him by violence, except that God cannot avenge his own wrongs?” To this the reply: On these utterly false and empty reasonings of yours, let the reins be loosened and let go, and let every sin of human license be left unpunished. Let no barrier of laws be set up, and let reckless harm-doing and lustful wantonness run riot. Let no king restrain his kingdom, no general his soldiers, no governor the people of his province, no master his slave, no husband his wife, no father his son from the freedom and sweetness of sinning by any threats or penalties. Take away what sound doctrine wisely says through the apostle for the health of the whole world. And, to strengthen the children of perdition in a choice that is worse the freer it is, delete what the chosen vessel says: “Let every soul be subject to the higher authorities. For there is no authority except from God, and those that exist have been ordained by God. Therefore whoever resists authority resists God’s ordinance, and those who resist bring judgment on themselves. For rulers are not a terror to good work, but to evil. Do you want to be free from fear of authority? Do good, and you will have praise from it. For it is God’s minister, an avenger in wrath on the one who does evil.” Delete these words if you can, or, if you cannot delete them, despise them, as you do. Make the worst possible choice about all of this, so that you may not lose your free choice. Or at least, since you are men and feel shame before men, cry out if you dare: “Let murders be punished, let adulteries be punished, let all other crimes and outrages of wickedness or lust, however great, be punished. Only sacrileges do we want left unpunished by the laws of rulers.” Or are you saying anything else when you say: “It is a great insult to God if he is defended by men. What does someone think of God when he wants to defend him by violence, except that God cannot avenge his own wrongs?” When you say this, what else are you saying but: “Let no human authority oppose or interfere with our free choice when we do wrong to God”? What a pity! The ancient times were cheated of such teaching, because you were not yet born when holy Moses bore the wrongs done to himself most gently but avenged those done to God most severely. Now you, made more learned by heretical presumption, cry out with the most odious appeal: “God made man and left him in the hand of his own choice. Why is human authority now snatching from me what God has bestowed?” Plainly you are demanding that, so you can do wrong to God, who made man with free choice, men should leave you your free choice. But there were also those forbidden by King Nebuchadnezzar’s decree, under the terrible threat of their own destruction and the ruin of their houses, to blaspheme the God of Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, and who would be sharply punished if they ignored it. They too could have said what you have said: “It is a great insult to God if he is defended by men. What does someone think of God when he wants to defend him by violence, except that God cannot avenge his own wrongs?” They could have spoken these very words of yours, and perhaps they did, if not with the same freedom, then with no less emptiness.

So free choice was given to man when he was created, but on the condition that if he did evil he would suffer for it. Indeed, when those first human beings sinned, they were condemned to death. And before the final death of the body was also completed in them, they were sent into exile from paradise. The emperor, out of Christian gentleness, has decreed milder penalties against you: he chose to impose exile on you, not death. But you are learned men. You consider what your deserts call for and how far short of it the punishment falls, and so you add death, not by his judgment but by your own. Do not perish forever by wanting men to grant you free choice in this life to offend God. Listen to the apostle and you will have a great shortcut, so that royal power cannot harm you: “Do good, and you will have praise from it.” The righteous before us also had praise from it. This includes not only those who faithfully obeyed religious kings, but also those who endured ungodly kings as enemies for the sake of God’s truth. The first had the praise of obedience, the second the praise of suffering. Yet both had it from that authority, and they had it by doing good, not by resisting the authorities. What you are doing is not only not good; it is a great evil. You tear apart the unity and peace of Christ. You rebel against the promises of the gospel. And you carry Christian standards, as if in a civil war, against him of whom it was said: “He shall rule from sea to sea, and from the river to the ends of the earth,” that is, against the true and supreme King of Christians. So let it be enough of an opportunity for your correction that, for such great evils of yours, you receive far milder and lesser penalties, provided you do not inflict on yourselves of your own accord what the emperor has not decreed. And do not wish men to grant you free choice for licentious impunity, or you may fall more wretchedly into the hands of God himself. For your own forebears also judged that in such wrongs against God, human free choice should not be left unpunished by kings. Though their cause was bad, they pursued Bishop Caecilian until they brought him to the judgment of the Emperor Constantine.

The words of the letter: “But our faith,” he says, “which the Lord Christ left to the apostles, is made most precious to us by these persecutions alone. ‘You will be blessed,’ he says, ‘when men persecute you and revile you and say every evil against you for the sake of the Son of Man. Rejoice and be glad, for your reward is great in heaven; for so their fathers persecuted the prophets who were before you.’ If this was said only to the apostles, faith had its rewards only up to them, and what good was it to those who would believe later? So it is clear that it was said to all. Then the apostle Paul says: ‘Those who wish to live holily in Christ must suffer persecution.’ And the Lord said this in the gospel: ‘The hour will come when everyone who kills you will think he is offering a sacrifice to God. But they will do these things because they have not known the Father or me.’” To this the reply: You would rightly say these things in seeking the glory of martyrs if you had the cause of martyrs. For the Lord does not call blessed those who suffer these evils, but those who suffer them for the sake of the Son of Man, who is Christ Jesus. But you do not suffer for him; you suffer against him. You suffer because you do not believe in him, and you endure it so as not to believe. How then can you boast that you hold the faith that the Lord Christ left to the apostles? Do you want people to be so blind and deaf that they do not read or hear the gospel, where they can learn what faith about his Church the Lord Christ left to the apostles? You are divided and separated from that Church, and you do nothing but rebel against the words of the Head and the Body. And yet you boast that you endure persecution for the sake of the Son of Man and the faith he left to the apostles. Let us leave other passages aside and hear his last words on earth. There let us see what faith about the Church he left to the apostles, and what testament, so to speak, he made. He did not make it as one about to end his life but as one who would live without end, not as one to be laid in a tomb but as one about to ascend into heaven. When he rose from the dead, he appeared to his disciples to be seen with their eyes and touched with their hands, and he said: “Everything written about me in the law and the prophets and the psalms had to be fulfilled.” Then he opened their minds to understand the Scriptures, and he said to them: “For thus it is written, and thus it was necessary for the Christ to suffer and to rise on the third day, and for repentance and forgiveness of sins to be preached in his name to all nations, beginning from Jerusalem.” Likewise on the Mount of Olives, after which he said nothing further while he was on earth, he commended this last as what was most necessary. For many people throughout every part of the earth were going to claim the name of the Church for themselves. Each of them would bark from the corners of their own ruins against the whole house, which sings a new song throughout the whole earth, the song of which it is written: “Sing to the Lord a new song; sing to the Lord, all the earth.” The apostles wanted to hear something else and did not ask about what they most needed. “Tell us,” they said, “will you at this time restore the kingdom to Israel?” He said: “It is not for you to know the times or seasons that the Father has set by his own authority. But you will receive power when the Holy Spirit comes upon you, and you will be my witnesses in Jerusalem and in all Judea and Samaria and to the ends of the earth.” When he had said this, a cloud took him up. He added nothing further to these words. The later he spoke them, the more firmly he fixed them in his hearers’ minds. This bride the Bridegroom entrusted to his friends as he departed. This, then, is the faith concerning the holy Church that he left to his disciples. You Donatists resist this faith, and yet you claim that you endure persecution for the faith the Lord Christ left to the apostles. This Son of Man commended his Church with such great care, a Church beginning from Jerusalem and bearing fruit and growing among all nations. You contradict him with astonishing, blind shamelessness, and yet you cry out that you suffer evils for the sake of the Son of Man. Or do you perhaps say this because you have found yourselves another son of man, by whose name you are called and to whose party you are said to belong? You are mistaken; he is not the one. When that Bridegroom said that suffering persecution for the sake of the Son of Man is blessedness, he was proclaiming himself, not an adulterer.

We too admit, as you say, that “You will be blessed when men persecute you” was not said to the apostles alone. It applies to all, though not to all who after them have suffered, are suffering, or will suffer any kind of persecution, but to those who suffer it for righteousness’ sake, as the apostles did. For a little earlier he had said: “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.” Then he added the words you chose to cite and to claim for yourselves in vain. It is in vain that you think this blessedness belongs to you, since you show no righteousness in yourselves for a reward to be owed to. On the contrary, you suffer for your wickedness, less at the hands of others and more at your own. So even before God’s judgment, which is still to come, you yourselves pay back to yourselves some part of what you deserve. You yourself said that this was spoken not to the apostles alone but to all, so that faith would not seem to have had its rewards only up to them. Then just as this was said not to the apostles alone but to all who after them would suffer any evils for righteousness’ sake, so too this was said to all: “If they persecute you in this city, flee to another.” Why do you not do this, if you belong to the company of those to whom these words were spoken? Even if you did it, that would not make you belong to them, since robbers whom the public laws have ordered to be hunted down can do the same. Yet because you refuse to do it, you show at once that you do not belong to those to whom these words were spoken. And your own excuse shows you even more plainly to be strangers to the number of true Christians. You say that you already lack places to take refuge in, though he promised that they would not be lacking until the end of the age. In this way you in no way prove that he made false promises. Instead you show that you do not belong to the company of those to whom he made this promise. And so you are not true martyrs but deceitful heretics. What more need we say to you, when your own tongue defeats you?

You also added that the apostle said: “All who wish to live godly in Christ must suffer persecution.” He did not actually say “must,” but: “All,” he said, “who wish to live godly in Christ will suffer persecution.” But who doubts that you do not belong to these? For if you too are among those of whom the apostle said this, why do you not do what the apostle himself did? If the gates were shut against you, you should have been let down over the wall to escape the hands of your persecutors. The gates stand open, and you will not go out. What persecution do you suffer except from yourselves? Your persecutor loves you, and your own frenzy persecutes you. He wants you to flee; it drives you to destruction. Besides, if you understand the apostle’s words “All who wish to live godly in Christ will suffer persecution” in this way, you must admit that your forebears did not live godly lives under the apostate emperor Julian. For anyone who became a Donatist in that time and died before the godly concern of Christian emperors rose up against your error once more did not live a godly life, since he did not suffer persecution. But the apostle may have said this because, as it is written elsewhere, “The life of man on earth is a trial,” and the devil never stops testing godly and true Christians, not only by the assaults of adversity but also by the seductions of prosperity, so that the human mind either gives way under affliction or comes to nothing through pride. If so, then surely, as long as we live here, all who wish to live godly in Christ will suffer persecution, so that either they are defeated and taken captive by the devil or, proven true, they defeat the devil. But those whom he already holds as caught and captive he does not persecute in order to gain them. Since he already has them, he makes use of them.

Moreover, suppose we should call a persecutor only someone who torments with some pain, or who wants to seize a person in order to torment him. Then do not think that one who torments the heart is less serious than one who torments the body. Consider what kind of persecution was suffered by the one who said in the psalm: “I saw the senseless, and I wasted away.” Righteous Lot suffered this persecution in Sodom, even before the men of Sodom tried to violate the angels who were his guests in his house, thinking they were men. For the righteous man could not see those people so publicly shameless without great torment of heart, even before the outrage against his own house.

That is why the apostle Paul, among his persecutions, also mentions things like these, saying: “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is made to stumble, and I do not burn?” So the greater the love of Christ in us, the greater the grief of heart with which we see you holding the sacraments of Christ while you are cut off from the members of Christ and rebel against the peace of Christ. Yet as long as you live in this body, we are given some hope concerning you [?]; but when you die still in that division, we grieve for you far more bitterly. And further, when you kill yourselves, whether by rushing on other people's weapons or by your cliffs, drownings and fires, words cannot express how much sorrow you torment us with. Indeed, the wicked Absalom grieved his holy father David more by his death than by his rebellion. For David wanted him taken alive, so that one who was rampaging in malice might be healed by repentance. So Absalom persecuted his father not only by dividing the people of God, and not only by bearing arms and making war against the law of God and against his father's lawful kingship, but far more did he persecute his father's heart by dying in that wickedness. In the end that best of fathers, who had not wept for his worst of sons while he lived, because he had not despaired of him, wept for him once he was killed and hope was at an end. Learn, then, what the apostle means when he says: “All who wish to live godly lives in Christ will suffer persecution.” If the Donatists had not plundered the houses of Catholics, if they had not burned Catholic churches, if they had not thrown the holy books of Catholics into those very fires, if they had not afflicted the bodies of Catholics with the most savage beatings, if they had not cut off the limbs of Catholics, if they had not put out their eyes, if in the end they had not cruelly killed Catholics, we would say with complete truth that this alone is the most grievous persecution we suffer from you: that we see you senseless and waste away, see you weak and are weak ourselves, see you made to stumble and burn, see you lost and mourn. These evils of yours, which are sending you to eternal ruin, persecute us more bitterly than those that you inflict on our bodies or property, our houses or basilicas. You persecute us less when you rage against us than when you perish. Indeed, in the persecution by which you rage against us we rejoice and are praised; but in this one, by which you perish, if we were to rejoice we would perish with you. Yet as long as you live in this flesh, we cannot despair of you [?]; but when you die in this wickedness, above all when you kill yourselves in the horrifying blindness of your frenzy, our most bitter sorrow is consoled by the one thing that consoled holy David: namely, that the people of God, who had been divided by the tyranny of his criminal son, was gathered together again in unity. For it is far more bearable that a much smaller number of your most obstinate members should perish by their own cliffs, drownings or fires, than that countless peoples, while those men stand in the way of their salvation, should burn with them in the blaze of eternal fire. So the Church of Christ has never lacked, and never will lack, the means by which, as the apostle says, those who wish to live godly lives in Christ suffer persecution: either by enduring the malice of the wicked while they live in harmful ways, or by grieving for them when they perish.

So do not be deceived by the fact that it was said to us: “The hour will come when those who kill you will think that they are doing God a service,” or, as you have cited this text, “will think that they are offering a sacrifice to God.” It is plain, of course, that this was not said about the persecutions that the Gentiles inflicted on the church. For when the Gentiles did this, they reckoned that they were doing service to their many gods, who do not exist at all, while they did this to the one God [?]. So this same thing which the Lord foretold to his own was either fulfilled through the Jews, who killed St Stephen and many others while they thought they were doing God a service, since they were seen to worship the one true God; or else it was said to us too, that is, to Catholics, about the various heretics raging everywhere, who, wherever they can, whenever they can and however they can, think that they are doing God a service by killing Catholics. Above all it was said about you, who have made yourselves a special name in Africa from such victims. For if it had been said to you, you would certainly not kill yourselves; you would rather wait to be killed by us, who, as you say, think that we are doing God a service when we do it. But as it is, when you hurry to your death so as not to be held by our people, it is living that you fear, not being killed, because you are ashamed to be corrected or to be convicted of your error. Or are you perhaps the ones to whom both apply, since, when you are killed, and killed by yourselves, you think that you are doing God a service and offering him these victims from among yourselves? To you, then, applies what follows, which you also quoted. For the Lord immediately added: “But they will do these things to you because they have not known the Father or me.” So when you kill yourselves, thinking that you are doing God a service, you have not known the Father, whom you have not heard saying, “You shall not kill,” nor have you known the Son, whom you have not heard saying, “Flee.”

The words of the letter: “But they boast,” he says, “that they dwell in a war-making peace and a bloody unity. Let them hear the Lord saying: ‘My peace I give to you, my peace I leave with you; not as the world gives do I give to you.’ For the world’s peace is concluded with arms and the outcome of war between the minds of nations at variance; the peace of the Lord Christ, calm in its wholesome gentleness, invites the willing and does not compel the unwilling.” To this the reply: It is you who want to make a war-making peace and a bloody unity, either by our violent deaths or by your own voluntary deaths, not holding yourselves to account for what you do to us, and holding us to account for what you do to yourselves. But we are forced to bear what you do to us, and we can do nothing but grieve over what you do to yourselves, provided only that the peace and unity of Christ come about for the salvation of many, as it does come about in very many, even if, because of the madness of a few, it does not come about in all. For if you were willing to look with a faithful eye rather than an envious one, you would see how truly the peace and unity of Christ are a joy to those who have come over from you to us, the ranks of so many great peoples. Even if some among them are still unsettled by the very novelty of it, they too are gradually being healed of this weakness. And if some persist in pretence, surely those whom we see to be sincere were not to be left ungathered because of them; and some of these sincere ones in your regions have even shown themselves greater than some of our own people, when, though you were granted that freedom which leads to perdition, they refused to go back to you. So, in order not to lose these, we had to gather the pretenders as well, since we read in the gospel that the servants gathered guests both good and bad to their lord’s wedding feast. This is all the more so because the spirit of pride, like a wicked wind, blew you off the Lord’s threshing floor before the time of winnowing, and so we are trying, as far as we can with God’s help, to call you back to it. And you surely know how, when grain is swept back onto the threshing floor by the brooms of diligence, some earth is dragged along with it.

As for your view that the unwilling are not to be compelled to the truth, you are mistaken, not knowing the scriptures or the power of God, who makes them willing while they are compelled against their will. Were the Ninevites unwilling in their repentance just because they did it at their king’s compulsion? The prophet had already proclaimed God’s wrath to the whole city as he walked through it for three days. What need was there, then, for a king’s command that they should humbly entreat God, who looks not at faces but at hearts, unless there were some among them who would neither heed nor believe the divine warnings unless they were frightened by earthly power? So by this command of royal power, against which your voluntary downfall takes place, an occasion is given to many for the salvation that is in Christ. Even if they are brought by force to the supper of so great a householder and are compelled to enter, once inside they find reason to rejoice that they entered. For the Lord himself foretold that both things would happen, and he has fulfilled both. For when certain people had been rejected, who are clearly understood to be the Jews, since they had earlier been invited through the prophets and at the appointed hour preferred to make excuses, the Lord said to his servant: “Go out into the streets and lanes of the city, and bring in here the poor and the crippled and the blind and the lame.” And the servant said: “Lord, what you commanded has been done, and there is still room.” And the lord said to the servant: “Go out into the roads and hedges, and compel them to come in, so that my house may be filled.” We understand the “roads” as heresies and the “hedges” as schisms; for in this passage roads signify divergent opinions, and hedges perverse opinions. Why then are you surprised if anyone who does not enter this supper, neither brought in willingly nor driven in by force, dies of hunger, not for bodily food but for spiritual?

The words of the letter: “We rejoice,” he says, “in the hatred of the world. Under its pressures we do not give way but are glad. This world cannot love the servants of Christ, since it is known not to have loved Christ, as the Lord himself says: ‘If the world hates you, know that it hated me before you. If they persecuted me, they will persecute you too.’” To this the reply: How can you rejoice in the hatred of the world, not give way under its pressures but be glad, when you want to kill yourselves so as not to suffer troubles of any kind, and choose to die, not killed by others for the truth of Christ, but by yourselves for the party of Donatus? That is the insanity of circumcellions, not the glory of martyrs. Since your deeds are plain to see, why do you lay claim to words that belong to others? “This world,” he says, “cannot love the servants of Christ, since it is known not to have loved Christ.” Then we do not belong to this world, since we love you; but you are not servants of Christ, for you repay good with evil, and when you cannot exercise your malice on us you turn it back on yourselves, so that you neither love us and you kill yourselves. And when the Lord said: “If the world hates you, know that it hated me before you. If they persecuted me, they will persecute you too,” he said it not to you but to those whom he instructed that, if they were persecuted in one city, they should flee to another, which you do not do. He said it to those for whom cities to flee to would never be lacking until the end of the world, whereas you complain that such cities are already lacking for you, and you will not admit that you are not the people to whom these words were spoken.

The words of the letter: “But even if persecution should die down,” he says, “from what source is the number of martyrs being made up? For John says: ‘I saw the souls of those who had been slain, under the altar of God, crying out and saying: How long, O Lord, will you not judge and avenge our blood on those who dwell on the earth? And each of them was given a white robe, and they were told to rest a little while longer, until the number of their brothers should be completed, who were to begin to be killed as they themselves had been.’” To this the reply: If you wanted to be martyrs under Christ’s altar, you would not make a sacrifice to the devil by burning yourselves. For who rejoices at this madness of yours except the devil, who breathes it into you, and those who are on his side? It is he who sometimes threw that boy we read of in the gospel into the water and sometimes into the fire; it is he who drowned that herd of pigs, sending them headlong into the waves; it is he who, with a most audacious temptation, suggested even to the Lord himself that he throw himself down from the pinnacle of the temple. Beyond doubt you belong to the devil, since you resort so often in your deaths to these three kinds of death: water, fire and the precipice. For if you had not lost your minds to madness, the very words you have quoted from the holy book ought to call you back from the destruction you bring on yourselves. For what do the souls of the martyrs under God’s altar say? “How long, O Lord, will you not judge and avenge our blood on those who dwell on the earth?” They ask that their blood be avenged, and surely on those by whom it was shed. On anyone else? And so your blood will be avenged on you.

What could be more foolish than your thinking that this prophecy about the martyrs who were foretold to come has been fulfilled only in the Donatists, as if, after blessed John wrote this, no martyrs were killed until the party of Donatus arose, people who, whenever they cannot kill others, kill themselves, who do the works of robbers and demons and claim for themselves the glory of martyrs? Even if, in so long a span of time, that is, from John until these people, no true martyrs had been killed, we would say, if nothing else, that they would come in the times of Antichrist, when that number of martyrs would be completed. Still we would not believe that these men, guilty of the blood of others or of their own, add to the number of the true martyrs, who were told to rest a little while, until the number of their brothers should be completed, who were to begin to be killed as they themselves had been: killed, that is, by others, not by themselves like these men; and therefore these men are not “as they themselves had been.” We can also say with complete truth that the Catholics whom they kill in the times of the Donatists likewise belong to the filling up of that number. But since, after the apostle John, who wrote of those things to come, such a slaughter of martyrs has been carried out by the ungodly everywhere among so many nations, what do these men mean, these extorters of their own souls and torturers of others’, by boasting that what they read was foretold of the holy martyrs has been fulfilled in themselves? Prepare yourselves rather for your blood to be avenged, not on those who want either to take hold of you or to escape from you so that you may live, but on yourselves. Or is it perhaps to prevent this that you do not shed your blood, but instead dash it out by a fall from a height, or choke it in the water, or turn it to ash? But you are mistaken. It will be avenged on you, by whatever means you destroy it; indeed it would be avenged on you even if it were shed by others, not in the church of Christ but in the party of Donatus. Will you then cry out to God to avenge your blood, and will he hear you without condemning you? For how can it be avenged unless the one who dared to slaughter it is condemned? In this cry, then, you are nothing but your own accusers, since you are guilty of your own blood, and God will condemn no one but you when he avenges your blood, whether you have dashed it, choked it, burned it, slaughtered it in any way at all, or, if you so choose, shed it.

The words of the letter: “Is this not persecution,” he says, “which has driven so many thousands of innocent martyrs to their death? For Christians, according to the gospel willing in spirit but weak in flesh, found a shortcut by way of the furnaces away from sacrilegious contamination and snatched away their own souls, imitating the example of the elder Razis in the books of Maccabees; nor were their fears groundless, for whoever fell into their hands did not escape. But let them do as much as they like: what is certain is that those who act against God cannot be God’s.” To this the reply: You admit quite openly and quite truly what persecution you are suffering. It is the very one I have already spoken of, which is expressed clearly enough in the holy scriptures concerning certain ungodly people, of whom it is said that they suffer persecution from their own deeds. This could very fittingly be said of you even if the hands of others were slaughtering you for your sacrileges. For robbers, too, and any people guilty of capital crimes, when they are punished by just laws, are not to be said to suffer persecution except from their own deeds. But now, when Christian gentleness spares you and yet your madness rages against you so that, as you say, you find a shortcut by way of the furnaces and snatch away your own souls, it is utter shamelessness to deny that you suffer persecution entirely from yourselves, since you accomplish both things: that for which you would justly perish, and the perishing itself. You say there are so many thousands of people who do this, as if this too were not no small reason why Africa should be freed from this teaching of yours. For the kind of people whom you have been able to persuade of this evil are those who used to do these things before as well, especially when the licence of idolatry was seething everywhere, and they would rush upon the weapons of pagans celebrating their festivals. The young pagans used to vow to their idols how many each of them would kill. And these men, flocking together from every side, would throw themselves onto the hunting spears held out against them, like savage beasts before the hunters in an amphitheatre. They died raving, they were buried rotting, they were venerated deceiving. Besides this, there are huge rocks and fearful mountain cliffs made famous by the very frequent voluntary deaths of your people. They did this less often by water and fire; it was by precipices that huge herds of them were consumed. I am speaking of things very well known to the people of our time. For who does not know this class of people, restless in horrible crimes, idle from useful work, most cruel in the deaths of others, holding their own lives cheapest of all, terrorizing above all in the countryside, keeping away from work in the fields, and going round the country storehouses to get their food, from which they also took the name of circumcellions, the disgrace of the African error, notorious throughout almost the whole world?

Who, then, does not know how many of this class used formerly to go to their deaths by various means and perish, and how few, by comparison with them, now burn in their own fires? But if you think we ought to be moved because so many thousands die in this way, how much consolation do you suppose we have in the fact that far more thousands, beyond all comparison, are being set free from the great madness of the party of Donatus, in which not only the error of wicked division but this frenzy too has become law? For those who perish are not even equal in number to those of that same class who are now held by the order of discipline and who, having given up both the occupation and the name of circumcellions, devote themselves to cultivating the fields, keep chastity and hold to unity. How much less are these lost men equal in number to the people of both sexes, not only boys and girls, young men and maidens, but also married people and old people, countless numbers of whom are passing over from the wicked dissension of the Donatists into the true and catholic peace of Christ! For those who burn themselves are not even as many as the places full of people who are being rescued from the deadly plague of that error and madness through this effort to bring about unity. Can it really be, I ask you, a sound policy of mercy that all these people should be kept for the eternal punishments of hell together with those men, so that those men, who are very few by comparison with them, should not be burned up in the fires of their own furnaces? For we must strive with great effort and prayer that all may live with Christ; but if, because of the madness of some, this cannot be done, we must at least work so that not all perish with the devil.

Of course, searching the holy scriptures with great shrewdness to see whether you could produce anything in support of this insane doctrine of voluntary death, you think you have found something, because it is written in the gospel: “The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak,” as if everyone ought to kill himself for this reason, that he is too weak to endure sufferings at the hands of persecutors. You could not have said more quickly that your false martyrs are of the number of those of whom it is written, “Woe to those who have lost their endurance,” and do not belong at all to those to whom the Lord says, “By your endurance you will gain your souls.” And those of whom we read, “The spirit is willing, but the flesh is weak,” were overcome by sleep that was not of their choosing; they were not put to death by a death of their own choosing. Read carefully and pay attention to what you are saying. What about what the apostle says: “God is faithful, who will not let you be tempted beyond what you can bear, but with the temptation will also provide the way out, so that you may be able to endure it”? Are we then not to believe this apostolic truth, and ought we to treat ourselves as enemies because we cannot endure other enemies? Far be this from Christian hearts. Let Catholics believe the faithful apostle, or rather the faithful God himself, who does not allow his own to be tempted beyond what they can bear, but with the temptation also provides the way out, so that they may be able to endure; let the Donatists not believe it, and, so as not to go on forever disbelieving it, let them cease to be Donatists. For when people despair of obtaining endurance from the Lord in any suffering, and therefore look for the shortcut of the furnaces, where these men throw themselves, not indeed to the wild beasts, as the most blessed Cyprian says, but to the flames, though no one has condemned them, that is not counsel but frenzy, not wisdom but insanity. Let them keep their fires, these men who do not say of the Lord’s help: “For from him comes my endurance.”

Certainly holy Job, when he was rotting with an unbearable sore from head to foot and racked with monstrous pains, had this shortcut of yours ready to hand, but he refused to use it to rescue himself from such a life, full of horrible calamities, in which he undoubtedly remained. The power was certainly there, but justice did not permit it. It is in this sense that he says: “Oh that I could kill myself, or ask another to do this for me!” The just man said he could not do what could not be done in accordance with justice. The apostle uses the same way of speaking to the Galatians: “I bear you witness that, if it could have been done, you would have plucked out your eyes and given them to me.” For why could this not have been done, except that it could in no way have been done justly? So too the Lord, when through his angels he was urging righteous Lot, as he left Sodom, to hurry to Zoar, said: “For I cannot do anything until you go in there.” He said that he could not do what he undoubtedly could do by his power, but could not do by his justice. For the most patient Job could, if nothing else, have refused food or drink and so ended that wretched and horrible life; but he could not do this justly, since no one is permitted to kill himself, especially when he can flee in order to live. Would anyone doubt that that holy man, who said so much in his pains, could have asked someone to do this for him? For while he was in pain and rotting, he did not lack a hand with which to kill himself, nor did he lack a tongue with which to ask. He could certainly have asked his own wife to do it. Yet not even she suggested that this be done, though she wanted him to die through blaspheming God and so provoking his anger; and so, though with wicked counsel she urged him to say something against God, she still did not dare tell him to kill himself. The devil has more power over you, since he so easily persuades you of what he had been unable to persuade that foolish woman, whom he had kept back, when everything else was taken from Job, as his servant to deceive her husband. So that just man said he could not ask anyone to kill him, thereby showing, of course, that it was not permitted. For what cannot be done justly the just man cannot do, since by deciding to do it he first loses his justice, so that what the just man cannot do the unjust man can. So when he said, “Oh that I could kill myself,” it was as if he were saying, “Oh that it were just,” for then it could be done by a just man. For he did not wish injustice on himself in order to be able to do what only an unjust man can do; rather, he wished, if it were possible, that this might be justice. Since this could not be, that is, since this could not be justice, the just man could not do what only injustice would do. And so it is not unjust for a just man to wish for death when life is very bitter; but if God does not grant the death he wishes for, it will be just only to endure that very bitter life. In the same way it is not foreign to a just man to wish for life when a bitter death threatens; but when he sees that he cannot obtain it, he says what the Lord said, taking us into himself: “Yet not what I will, but what you will, Father.” These words, however, are for those whom persecutors seek out to make them do evil, not for those whom people who love them seek out to share good things with them; they are for those, I say, who suffer persecution for the sake of justice, not for those who inflict it on themselves for the sake of injustice.

So too that elder Razis, whom these people, lacking any examples for their crime, boast of having found in the books of Maccabees as a man to imitate, ought to have done what we read in the same writings that the seven brothers did, with their mother urging them on: once seized, and without turning away from the law of his Lord, he should have accepted whatever was laid upon him, endured it in pain, and kept patience in his humiliation. Because he could not bear humiliation at the hands of his enemies, the example he gave was plainly one not of wisdom but of folly, fit for imitation not by the martyrs of Christ but by the circumcellions of Donatus. And yet, if we look at it more carefully, you turn out to be far even from him. When he was already being seized by his enemies, he had no free way of escape. That is why he struck himself with a sword; and when he could not kill himself, he threw himself from the wall; then, when he could no longer live, still breathing and driving his body forward, he ran, drained of blood though he was, and reached a sheer rock. There he pulled out his entrails with both hands, tore them apart, scattered them, and fell dead. He was so surrounded by the crowd that he could not have escaped even if he could have lived. You, then, who neither listen to the Lord when he says, "Flee," nor imitate Razis, who wanted to flee and could not: since you do not take the one as your commandment, you plainly do not take the other as your example either. And what of the fact that by your own reasoning this Razis must without doubt be blamed? For you said that, because of the Gospel saying where the Lord says, "The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak," you fled to the shortcut of the furnaces, since, of course, you are too weak to endure the hands of your enemies if you were seized by them. Then can it be said of the man who wounded himself gravely with a sword, who after being wounded made for the wall, who threw himself headlong from it, and who afterwards could still run to the rock, stand on the rock, and pull out, tear and scatter his entrails, that his spirit was willing but his flesh weak? Not only did his spirit prove so willing, but his flesh so strong, that it is scarcely credible that he wanted and was able to do what he did. So this man ought to displease you, since by his strength he upsets the reasoning you build on your weakness. Further, if he had been able to flee but unwilling, and had piled up wood in his house, and when his enemies burst in to seize him had set fire beneath it and burned himself up together with his house, he would indeed have given you an example, but he would have earned great torment for himself. As it is, since he could not flee, he is perhaps somewhat less guilty of his own blood, because the death he inflicted on himself was one that the enemy was about to inflict on him once he was captured.

"But," you say, "Razis is praised by the authority of the holy scriptures." Praised how? Because he was a lover of the city. That could also be meant in a carnal sense, namely of that earthly Jerusalem which is in slavery with her children, not of the Jerusalem above, our free mother. He is praised because he kept continence in Judaism; but the apostle says that such things were loss and dung to him compared with Christian righteousness. He is praised because he was called the father of the Jews; this is all the more the reason why impatience at humiliation crept up on him, as on any human being, so that he preferred to die rather than be subjected to his enemies. It is said that he chose to die nobly; he would have done better to choose to die humbly, for so he would have died profitably. Those are the words in which the histories of the nations habitually give praise, but they praise the brave men of this world, not the martyrs of Christ. It is said that he manfully threw himself from the wall into the crowds; nor do we say that he did it like a woman. You, of course, who have made great progress from this example, have taught even your women to do it; and we admit that even they do it not like women but like men, yet not to their salvation, since not in faith. Finally, as for his being said to have called upon the Lord of life and spirit to give these back to him again, that is, his life and spirit, not even then did he ask for anything that distinguishes the good from the wicked. For God will give these back also to those who have done evil, not in the resurrection of eternal life but in the resurrection of eternal judgment. So this Razis is praised as a lover of the city, as a man of very good report, that is, of good reputation, because he was called father of the Jews and because he kept continence in Judaism. But as for this death of his, more astonishing than prudent, scripture narrated how it happened; it did not praise it as something that ought to be done. Our task, as the apostle admonishes, is to test all things, hold fast to what is good, and abstain from every form of evil.

Now the Jews do not hold this scripture, which is called Maccabees, as they do the law, the prophets and the psalms, to which the Lord bears witness as to his own witnesses, saying, "Everything written about me in the law and the prophets and the psalms had to be fulfilled." But it has been received by the Church, and not without profit, if it is read or heard soberly, above all because of those Maccabees who, as true martyrs for the law of God, suffered such shameful and horrible things from their persecutors. From this the Christian people might take note that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory to come that will be revealed in us, for whom Christ suffered, if those men endured such great things so very patiently for the law that God gave through his servant to people for whom he had not yet handed over his Son. Even this Razis offers something useful to readers: not only that the mind may be exercised in judging rightly what it reads, but also that the human mind, indeed the Christian mind, may take note how much ought to be borne from enemies out of the ardor of charity, when this man bore so much from himself out of fear of humiliation. But the ardor of charity comes down from the heights of divine grace, whereas fear of humiliation arises from love of human praise; and so the one contends through patience, while the other sins through impatience. We ought not, therefore, to approve by consenting to whatever we read in the scriptures that men did, even men praised by God's own testimony, but to discern by reflecting, applying a judgment that rests not, of course, on our own authority but on that of the divine and holy scriptures. These do not allow us to imitate or praise all the deeds even of those men to whom they bear good and outstanding testimony, if some of those deeds were not rightly done or no longer suit this present time. But as for things that were right then and are not right now, what need is there to discuss any of them in this question? For the matter under discussion, that someone should inflict death on himself, especially one who is allowed, or rather compelled, to live, belongs among those deeds which never could be right and never could have been, as we have already sufficiently shown.

So, however you may take the praise given to this Razis's life, his death has no wisdom to praise it, because it lacks the patience worthy of God's servants. Rather, it is fitted by that saying of wisdom which is one not of praise but of condemnation: "Woe to those who have lost endurance." For if you believe that all the deeds of those who are praised should be imitated, is this Razis better than David? Why then does no good person set before himself as something to imitate David's deed in desiring another man's wife and killing her husband, but rather as something to beware of and avoid? Is Razis better than Solomon? Would you like us, then, to hold up as an example to imitate his wantonness with women, by whose seductions he was led so far as to build temples for idols? Is Razis better than the apostle Peter? When he said, "You are the Christ, the Son of the living God," he was called blessed by the Lord, so much so that he was found worthy to receive the keys of the kingdom of heaven; and yet no one believes he should be imitated where, at that very moment, he was rebuked and heard: "Get behind me, Satan; for you do not have in mind the things of God, but the things of men." And to pass over these things, which the holy scripture of the Church has condemned in the plainest terms, let me mention also those things which are merely narrated and recorded there, with no verdict of praise or blame given either way, but which are left to us to judge. Is Razis better than Noah? Yet what sober man would praise that man for lying drunk? Is Razis better than Judah the patriarch? Yet who would approve of him, who would be pleased with him, whom would he not most rightly offend by that act of fornication, since, although he did not go in to his daughter-in-law knowingly, for he did not know it was she, he nevertheless went in to a woman he thought was a prostitute? Is Razis better than Samson? Dare to say, then, if you can, that the great and divine secret of strength which he had in his hair should have been betrayed to a coaxing little woman. As for his killing himself together with his enemies when he brought the house down upon himself and them, he wished to share with them the death which he was soon to suffer at their hands, since he could not escape. And indeed he did not do this of his own accord; it must be attributed to the Spirit of God, who used him to do, when the Spirit was present to him, what he could not do when the same Spirit was absent. So too with Abraham's deed when he was willing to sacrifice his son: since God commanded it, it was obedience; had God not commanded it, what would it have been but madness?

Taught by these sacred writings, the blessed Cyprian said in his confession that discipline forbids anyone to offer himself up. See how much evil you do when you choose to kill yourselves, you who would be undisciplined even if you chose to offer yourselves to others who wanted to do this to you. He whom you call Savior commands flight; the persecutor permits flight. What, then, do you follow, that you perish in your own fires, if not your own madness? And yet you say: "Is this not persecution, which has driven so many thousands of innocent people to death?" Show us how you are innocent, you who divide Christ and kill yourselves. Show us how you are driven to death, you for whom flight is both commanded by God and allowed by men. Show us how by the shortcut of the furnaces you snatch your souls from defilement, when by the sacrilege of the furnaces, as by a diabolical sacrifice, you rather make them utterly defiled. Ask Christ: he commands you to flee. Ask the tribune: he permits you to flee. If you could ask Razis himself, he would answer us: "I could not flee." So you have neither Christ the Savior, nor the tribune the persecutor, nor Razis as your authority.

As for your statement that your people, in killing themselves, did not fear without reason, since whoever fell into our hands or the hands of our people did not escape, I ask what it is that he did not escape. If death, why do you inflict it on yourselves with your own hands, if you fear it from ours? But clearly you are not speaking of death. For you yourselves know how much we want you to live; that is why you try to frighten us with your deaths. So if you mean that none of you who fell into our hands escaped our communion, would that you were telling the truth! For it would be a very happy thing for them not to escape the communion offered by Catholics, so that they might escape the damnation prepared for heretics.
