But you could have realized that what you say is false from your own Emeritus, who, when he came to us, was more easily convinced by the truth than compelled to join our communion. There are others too, lesser in reputation but equal in folly. For anyone who was equally vain, so that he became obstinate against the plainest truth out of a most perverse sense of shame, since he blushes to be thought inconstant, has gone away from us without sharing in Catholic communion. But you said, "Whoever fell into their hands did not escape," because you supposed that the very few who persistently resisted the plainest truth and went away would go unnoticed. But by your own reckoning you have done Emeritus a very grave injury, since in your eyes he has lost the credit for his hardness, as though he had wished in vain to be among the few who refused to consent to the truth, because he did not earn a place among those who escape notice. Which of us would not believe that you envy your colleague? Or, if you do not envy him, imitate him. Come to us as he did; hear what we say as he did; answer, if you can, what he could not answer; but if you are willing neither to answer nor to enter communion, go away as he did. Look, he went away from our hands unharmed; why do you say, "Whoever fell into their hands did not escape"? Look, he did not believe he would lack places where he could hide; why are you making plans to burn? Do you not yet see that it is rather you who do not belong to God and who act against God, not only by the common plague with which you resist the unity of Christ, but also, above all, in that you hasten to add even deaths to this great crime of yours?

Words of the letter: "But since," he says, "the office of an executor did not befit your prudence, I beg you to attend briefly. Solid truth, I think, is one thing, and an image of truth another. Since truth stands firm, established by its own strength, an idol or image is something that human presumption has made to resemble the true, to the injury of the true; yet falsehood can never prejudice truth. I call worshippers of images those who do not hold the truth; I consider a pagan under another name anyone who makes for himself what he worships. Hence it is public and open knowledge that, by threats or terror and frequent persecutions, Gabinius and those like him, torn from the freedom of nature, are known, faithless as they are, to have fashioned for themselves objects to venerate, to whose worship people are compelled against their will." Reply to this: You go on adding words of blasphemy to your madness, and dare to say that the Catholic Church is a human fabrication, the Church to which God says: "For I am the Lord who makes you; the Lord is his name." And so that we may know that it is this Catholic Church spread throughout the whole world, he continues and adds: "And he who delivers you, the God of Israel himself, shall be called God of the whole earth." This most evident work of God you call a human fabrication, and you do not reflect that you would in no way be separated from this Church, which God promised he would make throughout the whole earth, unless you were following a man. We follow him who said to Abraham: "In your seed all nations shall be blessed." We follow him who said to his Church the words I have just quoted: "I am the Lord who makes you; the Lord is his name; and he who delivers you, the God of Israel himself, shall be called God of the whole earth." Therefore, in holding to the Church, which spreads and grows through all nations and through the whole earth, we are certainly not following a human fabrication but a divine promise and a divine deed. What are you following, that you choose to be cut off from communion with this divine promise and divine work and to belong to the party of Donatus? Was it a man or God who told you that through the sin of Caecilian the promises of God perished from the whole world and remained in the party of Donatus? If God, read it to us from the law, the prophets, the psalms, the apostolic and gospel writings. Read it, if you can, as you utterly failed to do at our conference. But if men said these things, men of whom it is said, "They made firm for themselves an evil word," then there is your human fabrication, there is what you worship, there is what you serve, there is the reason you rebel, rave and burn.

But Gabinius and the others, who came to know this Church, chose it and held to it, wanting to possess together with the faithful not a human fabrication but a divine promise, foretold and fulfilled, refused to go on suffering for a human fabrication those very human hardships. For whoever, for the sake of the truth and unity of Christ, loses not just his property but even this life of his, provided it is others who take it away and kill him, truly has faith, truly has hope, truly has charity, truly has God; but whoever loses even the hem of his garment for the party of Donatus has no sense. What wonder, then, if wise men, seeing penalties and exile set before them to counter the most stubborn antiquity of a hardened custom, considered whether they ought to suffer these things for the party of Donatus against the Catholic Church, that is, for a human fabrication against a divine work; and saw that they certainly ought not; and recognized that what you call persecution was for them an occasion for correction; and did what is written: "Give a wise man an occasion, and he will become wiser"? You see, then, how pointlessly you said to a man who, by order of his most pious emperor, seeks your correction, that the office of executor did not befit his prudence. For what better befits a religious man in the service than that, in a cause in which he weighs to whom you mean to be a deception [?], he himself should become salvation for the many who are to be corrected?

Words of the letter: "To teach the people of Israel," he says, "almighty God gave the task of proclamation to prophets; he gave no command to kings. The Savior of souls, the Lord Christ, sent fishermen, not soldiers, to instill the faith." Reply to this: Listen, then, to the holy prophets and the holy fishermen, and you will not find the most religious kings troublesome. For I have already shown above that it belonged to the king's responsibility that the Ninevites should appease God, whose wrath the prophet had announced. So as long as you do not hold to the Church which the prophets foretold and the fishermen apostles planted, the kings who hold to it judge, quite rightly, that it belongs to their responsibility that you not rebel against it with impunity. For God had kings, too, among the prophets: holy David, as you cannot be unaware, was a king. Listen, then, to a king prophesying, and you will have no fear of any religious king's anger. Listen, I say, to the prophet king saying of Christ: "He shall have dominion from sea to sea, and from the river to the ends of the earth," and you will not fear a Christian king who is angry with you for blaspheming this Church, which, as a king prophesied, is displayed to the ends of the earth. For even King Nebuchadnezzar, though he was no prophet, restrained with religious severity those who blasphemed the God of Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego.

Words of the letter: "God," he says, "who alone can judge the living and the dead, never looked for the help of worldly soldiery." Reply to this: God does not look for the help of worldly soldiery when he rather bestows a benefit on kings, inspiring them to see to it that their Lord's command is carried out in their kingdom. For those to whom it was said, "And now, O kings, understand; be instructed, you who judge the earth; serve the Lord in fear," realize that their power must serve the Lord in such a way that those who refuse to serve his will are punished by that power. As for your stirring up resentment about soldiers: if this responsibility, as we have already shown, is demonstrated in the holy scriptures to belong to kings, through whom are they to carry it out against the rebellious circumcellions and their mad partners or leaders, if not through the soldiers under their command?

The words of the letter: “But they do not know this,” he says, “these squatters on other people’s property, who do not hear God saying, ‘You shall not covet your neighbour’s goods,’ nor the Holy Spirit saying through Solomon: ‘Then the righteous will stand with great boldness against those who have oppressed them and taken away the fruit of their labours. Seeing it, they will be troubled with dreadful fear, and will be amazed at the suddenness of an unhoped-for salvation, saying among themselves in repentance, groaning in anguish of spirit: These are the ones whom we once held in derision and made a byword of reproach. We fools thought their life madness and their end without honour. How is it that they are counted among the children of God, and their lot is among the saints? So we have strayed from the way of truth, and the light of righteousness did not shine on us. We wearied ourselves in the way of iniquity and destruction, and we walked through trackless deserts, but the way of the Lord we did not know. What did our pride profit us, or what did our boasting of riches bring us? All those things have passed away like a shadow.’ This faith, then, urges us to die gladly for God in this persecution.” To this the reply: Acknowledge your crime, and do not claim for yourselves a name that belongs to others. Scripture said: Then the righteous will stand with great boldness against those who have oppressed them and taken away the fruit of their labours. It did not say, ‘All who have suffered evils will stand,’ but, The righteous will stand; just as the Lord too, when he said, Blessed are those who suffer persecution, would have meant not only those who are crowned for their patient endurance in the Lord but also those who are punished by just laws, had he not added, for righteousness’ sake. Therefore, if you think that these words of the righteous, which are written, apply to you, first show whether you are righteous. For you have great things to air among your righteous deeds: the dividing of Christ, the tearing apart of Christ’s sacraments, the desertion of Christ’s peace, war against Christ’s members, accusations against Christ’s bride, the denial of Christ’s promises. These are your righteous deeds, on account of which, no doubt, you will stand with great boldness against those who oppressed you and took away the fruit of your labours! And when you begin to boast, among your righteous deeds, that you kill yourselves, what righteous man will be your equal? For then above all you will appear as people whose deaths must be avenged—but consider on whom: on those, surely, who killed you. So, in order to be avenged, you will be punished, and thus you will stand against yourselves. Above all you will stand against yourselves, you who shut yourselves up in furnaces and squeeze yourselves into cruel straits, so that whoever wants to help cannot get in, and whoever wants to escape cannot get out. Far be it, far be it, that they should stand with great boldness when they stand with so evil a conscience! Unless perhaps you think that God will be able to spare you then for your crimes precisely because you do not spare yourselves now. That is why some of your nuns who were pregnant threw themselves over cliffs, and as their wombs burst open, by the crime of murder they also laid bare the crimes of fornication, supposing that if they punished themselves in this way, God would no longer punish them at all. In the same way you too think that whatever abominations you have been able to commit—by the sacrilege of schism and heresy, or by plundering, mutilating, blinding and killing Catholics, and finally even by rebaptizing them—can be expiated by this manner in which you kill yourselves. But you are mistaken: Judas thought this too. Or do you also want to add this proof, by which we may know more certainly that it was rather your forebears who were the traditors, because you imitate the death of the traitor?

So you confirm from this too that the records are genuine—something you were unwilling contentiously to deny at the Conference—the records in which Secundus of Tigisis, who was then bishop of the first see in Numidia, pardoned confessed traditors; and with those whose crimes of handing over were manifest and confessed, and which he remitted to them in their presence at Cirta, he punished at Carthage, as traditors, men who had not been convicted and were absent. And Secundus himself could not clear himself of that crime when Purpurius of Limata charged him with it, when the same Purpurius said to him: “What did you do, when you were held by the curator and the town council to make you hand over the scriptures? How did you get free of them, unless you handed over something or ordered something to be handed over? For they did not just let you go at random.” Now Secundus, in his letter to Mensurius as well, which you yourselves produced and read out, admitted without any ambiguity—not that he handed over, but that persecutors sent by the curator and council, as Purpurius of Limata charged him, came to him to make him hand over the scriptures; and that when they demanded them of him he answered, ‘I am a Christian and a bishop, not a traditor,’ and refused to hand them anything at all. You want us to believe him on this, although you yourselves see how incredible it is that, in the heat of that persecution, a bishop who had been detained or summoned to hand over the Lord’s scriptures was released without having handed any over. You certainly contended that bishops could not have come together at the city of Cirta to ordain a bishop in time of persecution. How then was that persecution raging, if a bishop could be held in order to hand over the scriptures and be released with impunity having handed over none? And yet, describing the savagery of the persecution of that time, you cried out that not even twelve bishops could have gathered in council to ordain a bishop and draw up those records—in which they mutually forgave one another the crimes of handing over and, for the sake of the Church’s peace, left them to the Lord to judge—while you, who say that at this time you are suffering such a persecution as there never was, so that you lack places to flee to and to hide in, nevertheless hold councils and ordain bishops, even, in the place of those who have perished in their own fires, others again of the same kind, ready to perish in their own fires. And in the time of so great a persecution, as you suppose and boast, you were able to gather in council even more than thirty, and Petilian was there too—the man who cried out that in time of persecution not even twelve could have gathered.

Moreover, in that very council you decreed that those, whether bishops or presbyters, who have entered communion with us against their will, provided only that they have not offered the sacrifice or preached to the people, are eligible for pardon and may be received back in their ranks; and so by this decree of yours you yourselves have entirely cut away the whole force of your slanders. For where now is your empty talk, in which you say that even those who were not traditors become traditors through our communion, because, as you slanderously claim, we were defiled by those who handed over the church’s books under pressure from the impious authorities of that time? Why then do you now acquit of the crime those whom you know to have entered communion with us unwillingly, provided they have not offered the sacrifice or preached a sermon to the people? As if those first traditors back then, under the terror and horror of monstrous tortures—such as no one at all has inflicted on you now—handed over the holy books willingly, or offered the sacrifice there, or preached a sermon to the people! You see, then, that just as you were able to pardon these men—whom you most groundlessly accuse of becoming traditors through our communion—if they did something against their will, so too your forebears were able, by the same rule, to pardon the real traditors who handed over under a far more pressing necessity. But they were driven by the faction of Caecilian’s enemies to condemn others who were absent and unheard, doing what the apostle says of such people: For in passing judgement on another you condemn yourself, for you who judge are doing the very same things.

Therefore, since the Donatists have always loved to kill themselves, and were themselves traditors from the beginning, what wonder if they have taught their descendants as well to love the traitor’s death? To avoid that likeness, it is true, they have never, or only very rarely, killed themselves with a noose—but entirely in vain. For the one who drove Judas the traitor to do it is the same who often threw that boy whom the Lord healed into water and fire, who hurled the herd of pigs into the sea, and who with bold presumption suggested to the Lord himself that he throw himself down from the pinnacle of the temple. So although you hurl yourselves into a voluntary death in various ways, nevertheless, by the prompting of the same devil, in killing yourselves you imitate the traitor. And even if you are not traditors yourselves, yet from the wicked teaching of those who were, and who made the schism in which you gladly remain, you have learned to do even this to yourselves which the traitor did to himself. See now with what righteousness you will stand against those who oppressed you: if your deaths are to be avenged, they can be avenged with perfect justice only on yourselves.

And what are these labours of yours that you loudly complain are being taken from you? Is it unjust that churches which were yours, when they pass over into Catholic peace, should pass over with their property? For if, when they come over to us, you want to keep their property, then beyond doubt it is you who want to take what belongs to others. But the Catholic mother says to you what the blessed apostle said to certain people: For I seek not what is yours, but you. And yet how can you fail to contradict yourselves, when you charge us with both things—that we want to possess your property, and that we force you by violence to be with us? You do not see how contradictory these two things are. For if we seek you and hold you in our communion against your will, how can we be after your property, which we certainly cannot have once you are in communion with us? And if we want to get hold of it, how can we be seeking you, so as to lose it once you are in communion with us? But we confess it to you: our greed is called charity. It is this that seeks you in us; it is this that longs to find you, to correct you and to join you together in the unity of Christ; it is with this fire that we burn when we fear that you will burn in your furnaces; it is this that kindles us, so that not only do we not covet your property, but we desire that you should possess ours together with us. Recognize this, and come, and do not choose to perish. Or if you are ashamed to come of your own accord, we serve your weakness so that nothing may be lost to charity. Look, we want to hold on to you: why are you in such a hurry to burn? We hold you for life, we hold you for salvation, we hold you for the unity, truth and sweetness of Christ; and to the supper of so great a householder, if you will not come in of your own accord, we compel you.

The contest is about righteousness, not money. So beware lest, while you think that what is written applies to you—Then the righteous will stand with great boldness against those who have oppressed them and taken away the fruit of their labours—this may not happen to you regarding your labours, but rather what is written in another place: The righteous will eat the labours of the ungodly. For the Maximianists, whose basilicas you took away whenever you could, will not stand against you; nor will the pagans stand against you, whose temples you certainly overthrew wherever you could, and whose basilicas you destroyed—which we too have done; nor will the musicians of the demons stand against you, whose pipes and foot-clappers you broke—which we too have done. In the same way, neither will you stand against us. For in all such actions it is not plunder that is coveted, but error that is overthrown. So just as the Canaanites will not stand against the Israelites, although the Israelites took away the fruit of their labours, whereas Naboth will stand against Ahab, because it was a crime committed, not a command given, that the unjust man should take away the labours of the just man, so heretics will not stand against Catholics when the orders of the Christian empire are carried out concerning the property of heretics—property which is not taken away by Catholics but rather is searched out and, as far as possible, kept to be returned in large part to them once they are corrected. But Catholics will stand not only against the gentiles, by whom the true martyrs were despoiled, but also against the Circumcellions of the Donatists, because they too took away the fruit of their labours. Yet with these monetary labours the case is easier, since even those to whom they belonged are passing over to Catholic peace. Look, every day, if anyone comes over to us, we give back your people’s money, clothes, crops, vessels, lands and houses. How will you give back to us the limbs of our people?

Surely at some point you will wake up and see that neither are you the ones of whom it is said, nor we the ones by whom it is said: These are the ones whom we once held in derision—since rather we hold you in tears. Nor will you be counted among the children of God unless you withdraw from the party of Donatus and hold to this Church which the Son of God displays, just as he foretold; nor is your lot among the saints, but among the heretics. As for your supposing that others will say of you, We fools thought their life madness, I am amazed that you are such fools that you do not say such things to yourselves now. It is to the true saints and faithful, indeed, that the unclean and unbelieving will say these things then—to those, that is, whom they now think mad, because they refuse to enjoy the pleasures they see, while they believe what they do not see. But as for you, if you do not think your life madness, then at least if you do not think this death of yours, which you wish to inflict on yourselves, madness, you are more desperately mad still. Those words, however—So we have strayed from the way of truth, and the rest—will not indeed be yours alone, but they will very much be yours too. For you are straying, as is plain, from the way of truth, and the light of righteousness does not shine on you; you are wearying yourselves in the way of iniquity and destruction, and you walk through trackless deserts, but the way of the Lord you do not know. As for what follows—What did our pride profit us, or what did our boasting of riches bring us? All those things have passed away like a shadow—I do not know whether anyone among the rest could say it more aptly and fittingly than your predecessor Optatus. So do not imagine yourselves to be what you are not, and perish as what you are; for it is not this faith but your evil error that urges you—not to die gladly for God in this persecution, as you say, but to suffer persecution for your deeds, wickedly, on behalf of Donatus.

The words of the letter (and in another hand): “I wish,” he says, “that you, keeping well, having perceived the truth, may soften your mind and refrain from the exits of innocent people.” To this the reply: It is rather you who should perceive the truth and soften your minds, so that they do not rage so fiercely as not to spare even yourselves. For what gentler man could easily be found than this man to whom you wrote this, who both invited you to life and, if you would not live it with us, let you go free to flee? It is you who are harsh towards yourselves, you who are ruthless, you who are cruel without any regard for humanity, who do to yourselves what lovers of errors and persecutors of human beings are accustomed to do to their enemies, so that the persecutors of errors and lovers of human beings have cause to grieve most bitterly. And why do you wish that he should refrain from the exits of the innocent? You are certainly not innocent; yet he gave you an exit, but you want to give yourselves extinction. For I think ignorance of the word misled you, so that, wanting “extinctions” to be understood, you said “exits.” So when you urge, by your wish, that the executor of the imperial laws should refrain from the extinction of the innocent, what you are doing is getting him to spare the deceivers and let the innocent be deceived with impunity. What else, then, but that this man, for whom you think you are wishing well, should keep faith neither with God nor with his emperor—because, of course, according to a justice not true but yours, cases of this kind ought not to concern the emperors so that a slanderous division might be healed, but ought to have concerned them when the division was made, so that it might be confirmed? If this doctrine, which you have learned not from the holy scriptures but from who knows where—that these matters do not belong to the imperial power—seems just to you, then it should have occurred to your forebears when they sent the case of Caecilian, as his accusers, to the judgement of the emperor Constantine. But now, since the lions did not harm Daniel because of his innocence, you want them to spare those who by their slanders threw him to the lions. But God does not judge as man judges—God in whose hand is the heart of the king, and he turns it wherever he wills. When the king’s heart is unbelieving, the good are either exercised or proved; but when it is believing, the wicked are either corrected or punished. Which of these two applies in your case we have already said sufficiently, and we have answered your letter sufficiently, passing over no part of it; and we trust that, by the Lord’s mercy, this will be of benefit at least to some of you—and would that it might be to you as well!

But if you are preparing some reply to this, read also the proceedings held with Emeritus, to which he himself could not reply, to see whether perhaps you can, as I already advised you above to try. We also dealt with him on the case of the Maximianists, about which, though it was put to you by us so many times at the Conference, you made no reply, since on a matter so very plain and so very recent you could find nothing to reply: how is it that Maximian—whom you struck with a far heavier sentence than Caecilian, so that you called him a minister of Dathan, Korah and Abiram, whom the earth swallowed alive for the crime of schism—did not defile the partners of his schism, to whom you granted a period of grace to return to your communion; how is it that an African did not defile Africans, a living man the living, a known man those known to him, a partner his associates, and yet Caecilian defiled those overseas, defiled those far away, defiled those unknown to him, defiled those not yet born? Find, if you can, what to say about how you accepted the rank of Felician of Musti and Praetextatus of Assuras, whom you condemned together with Maximian and ten others without any period of grace, against whom you went to law before two—or, unless I am mistaken, three—proconsuls in order to drive them out of their basilicas, and whom, after you had already ordained another in Praetextatus’s place, you received back in their ranks after so long a time. By what justice, by what reason, with what face is a condemned Maximianist received in his rank, while the Catholic world is condemned unheard? By what justice, by what reason, with what face do you say that you must be on your guard lest you be defiled by Caecilian—long since dead and entirely unknown to you, condemned once with your forebears as judges, acquitted three times with your forebears as accusers—and yet you did not think you must be on your guard lest you be defiled by Felician, condemned by the mouth of your general council and received by all of you, chiefly through the favour of your predecessor? By what justice, by what reason, with what face do you annul the baptism given by the churches which the apostles planted by their labours, when you have accepted the baptism which Felician and Praetextatus conferred outside your church for so long a time, while you were going to law against them as condemned men? For if the scripture, He who is baptized by a dead man, what does he gain by his washing?, is to be understood in the way you usually misunderstand it and throw it at us, then these men, when they were baptizing, lay among those about whom your sentence at Bagai thundered with such a din: “Quite after the example of the Egyptians, the shores are full of the corpses of the perishing, for whom in death itself the greater punishment is that, after their life has been wrung out of them by the avenging waters, they do not even find burial.” What are you going to say to this? Look, the dead baptize those whom you receive, and you do not die; and yet you slander us as dead, so that, refusing communion with Catholic unity, you truly die in your own fires. Answer these things; you have leisure to think out what to say. Let us at least confer on you this benefit, that while you think about what to reply, you may think less about how to burn. But we do not want you, for lack of an answer, still to imagine that you must say that worn-out, battered line you are accustomed to say: ‘If we are such people, why do you seek us?’ For we answer: all the more ought the Catholic Church to seek you, because you are lost, if you, being lost, sought out the lost Maximianists. You speak to us from your own heart: ‘Why do you seek people guilty of so many and such great crimes?’ But we answer you from the book of God: because charity covers a multitude of sins.
BOOK TWO.

I have received your reply, Gaudentius, if it can be called a reply at all. You chose to send it to me so that we would not say you had been refuted, as we might have done if you had kept silent. But not keeping silent is not the same thing as replying. If it were, you have certainly replied. Yet you have replied in such a way that even those who might have had some hope of you will see that you could not find what you ought to answer, and answered anyway only so as not to stay silent. So in taking care not to be called beaten, you have made sure that you are shown to be beaten. Your own writings are enough to show this, if people of understanding read them and compare them carefully with mine. But to demonstrate it in a further piece of writing, so as to satisfy slower minds as well, a somewhat longer discussion is needed. I will indeed undertake it, if it proves necessary and the Lord wills.

Meanwhile, since you have tried to claim on the testimony of blessed Cyprian that you are the true catholics, pay attention for a moment to the kind of Church he called catholic when he was defending its unity. "The Church," he says, "flooded with the light of the Lord, sends forth her rays through the whole world. Yet it is one light that is spread everywhere, and the unity of the body is not divided. In her abundant fruitfulness she stretches her branches over the whole earth, and she pours out her generously flowing streams far and wide. Yet there is one head, one source, and one mother, rich in the offspring of her fruitfulness." Why, then, do you deceive yourselves and try to deceive others with shameless lies? If this martyr's testimony makes your church the catholic Church, show that it sends forth its rays through the whole world. Show that in its abundant fruitfulness it stretches its branches over the whole earth. This is why it is called by the Greek word "catholic." What is called holon in Greek is translated as "whole" or "universal" in Latin. So "throughout the whole" or "according to the whole" is kath' holon, and that is where the name "catholic" comes from. If you know this, why do you pretend not to? And if you do not know it, why do you not ask those who know before you speak about what you do not know? If you dislike this, then find some language other than Greek in which to prove that kath' holon does not mean "throughout the whole" or "according to the whole" or "according to the universal," and give up Cyprian's testimony. For he speaks against you, as you can see from what he says. He says that the catholic Church is spread out and extended through the whole world and over the whole earth, which agrees with its Greek name and definition. You are found holding, thinking and saying something different. And while you rest your case on Cyprian as your witness, Cyprian is the witness who proves you a liar.

This, then, is the true and genuine catholic Church. Flooded with the light of the Lord, it sends forth its rays through the whole world, and in its abundant fruitfulness it stretches its branches over the whole earth. When you are asked why you left it, you can find no just cause. No plausible excuse can wash away your departure from this Church. For what do you say except, "Necessity compelled us, so that we, the righteous, might leave the unrighteous"? Divine Scripture answers you: "A wicked son calls himself righteous, but he does not wash away his going out." "His going out," it says. This is surely the going out of which the apostle John says, "They went out from us." He does not wash it away at all. He does not defend it, excuse it, or cleanse it. In the catholic Church, the duty of the righteous is simply to bear with great patience the wicked whom they cannot correct or condemn. They must not leave before the time: not leave the Lord's field because of the tares, nor the Lord's threshing floor because of the chaff, nor the Lord's house because of the vessels meant for dishonor, nor the Lord's nets because of the bad fish. Otherwise they will try in vain to wash away their going out. If you try to twist these sayings of the Gospel into some other sense by any argument whatever, you contradict that same blessed Cyprian whose testimony you bring forward, just as you did at our conference. For these are the martyr's words on this question, in the letter he wrote to Maximus and his fellow confessors: "Although tares are seen to be in the Church, this ought not to hinder our faith or our love, so that we ourselves withdraw from the Church because we see that there are tares in it. We need only labor to be wheat, so that when the wheat begins to be stored in the Lord's barns, we may receive the fruit of our work and labor. The apostle says in his letter: 'In a great house there are not only vessels of gold and silver, but also of wood and clay, some for honor and some for dishonor.' Let us strive and labor as much as we can to be a vessel of gold or silver. But to break the vessels of clay is granted to the Lord alone, to whom a rod of iron has also been given. The servant cannot be greater than his lord. Nor may anyone claim for himself what the Father has granted to the Son alone, so as to think that he can already carry the fan or winnowing shovel to winnow and cleanse the threshing floor, or that he can separate all the tares from the wheat by human judgment. That is proud obstinacy and sacrilegious presumption, which a depraved madness takes upon itself. While certain people keep taking upon themselves more than gentle justice requires, they perish from the Church. And while they insolently exalt themselves, they are blinded by their own swelling pride and lose the light of truth."

Surely now at least you see that at our conference you cried out against holy Cyprian and resisted him with your arguments. You asserted that Christ's field, of which he says, "The field is the world," is not the Church but the world apart from the Church, so that the field could contain tares that are seen. For whenever we put forward this testimony of Cyprian, you kept saying that there could be no manifest tares in the Church. You did not dare to resist him openly, yet you were unwilling to agree with him. Surely now at least you are waking up, listening and taking note that "although tares are seen to be in the Church, this ought not to hinder our faith or our love, so that we ourselves withdraw from the Church because we see that there are tares in it." Why then do you depart from the unity of this Church in wicked schism, and persist in that same division with heretical presumption? Here you have Cyprian: agree with him or answer him. In these words he says that there are tares in the Church and that they are seen, and yet that no one ought to depart from the Church on that account. See how this wipes out all the slanders in your writings. In them you went so far over the edge, and threw yourself headlong as your party usually does, that you said Christians throughout the whole world could have perished through other people's sins even without knowing who had sinned. Your reason, of course, is that we read in the holy Scriptures that one man stole from what was under the ban, and that for his sin a people who knew nothing of it was punished. You failed to understand that those penalties on mortal bodies, that is, the deaths of people who were going to die anyway, served to put a salutary fear into the people. But other people's sins, especially sins they did not know of, did the dead no harm at all as regards the life to come. Would you really say this? Would you really dare to believe and say that anyone perishes before God through other people's sins, and even through sins he does not know of? Were you not at least afraid of your own colleagues? At our conference you kept silent, perhaps because you already held this view but did not dare to say it, while they fought with all the force of argument to show that the bad fish in the Lord's nets are unknown to the fishermen. Their point was that the fishermen would not perish by contact with them, as they would if they knew them. Do you not remember what happened when we were arguing about the chaff on the Lord's threshing floor, that is, the Church, which must be tolerated in one mixture until the time of winnowing? When Emeritus was pressed, he denied it and said, "You do not read 'threshing floor.'" His own people warned him privately, and we warned him openly, citing the Gospel: the Lord will come with his fan in his hand, he will cleanse his threshing floor, store the wheat in the barn, and burn the chaff with unquenchable fire. He at once corrected the lapse of memory that had led him to deny that this was written. Yet he did not turn away from the schismatic or heretical perversity by which he denied that the good must bear with the wicked for the sake of the Church's unity. Instead he at once said that the name "chaff" signified hidden wicked people. In this way your party could carefully preserve, as the chief point of your case, the principle that unknown wicked people could not defile any of the good. See how the distinguished advocate of your party has lost all his labor, with you opposing him. To protect the salvation of the good, he asserts that the wicked who remain in the Church are entirely unknown to the good, so that they do not destroy them, as they would if they were known and tolerated. You, on the other hand, have said that the good perish even through contact with wicked people who are unknown. Yet you have not feared the many hidden scoundrels, criminals and ungodly people your party has had from the beginning, who by your own reasoning have certainly destroyed you and all your people without your knowing it. Even now you have not trembled with fear that one of your people might be sinning without your knowledge and destroying you while you say these things. Or perhaps, since you understand that you have perished through your own known deeds, you see no reason to fear perishing through other people's unknown ones?

What should I wish for you, except that we may be allowed to find you, so that you may not choose to perish? Suppose your opinion is true, that each person perishes both through his own sins, which he commits, and through the sins of others, when he does not even know whether they have been committed. What hope would then remain? There would be none for us, who agree with Christ the Lord, the prophets, the apostles and holy Cyprian that even known wicked people must be borne for the sake of the bond of unity, if we can neither correct nor punish them. But there would be none for you either, who are pleased to separate yourselves bodily from the wicked before the time of the harvest, the winnowing and the shore. For if this is so, then your forebears too, who separated themselves (as you believe) from known wicked people, certainly perished through unknown ones. You say that a person perishes through other people's crimes whether he knows of them or not, and so you leave no one at all innocent. Emeritus himself holds a far more tolerable view: he entangles people in the sins of others through the communion of the sacraments only when those sins are known, and releases them from unknown ones. But the venerable Cyprian has answered both you and him with a far truer voice. He says that the wheat does not perish when it grows together with tares that stand not outside the Church but within it, and that are not hidden and unknown but plainly known and evident. For I think that someone who insists that what is seen is hidden is blind, not in body but in his very mind. When that most blessed man warns against withdrawing from the Church because of the tares in it, his warning is not about tares that are hidden, but rather about those that are seen. These are the ones that can disturb those who see them, unless wisdom makes them patient. For how could we be taught not to withdraw because of hidden tares, when we do not know that they exist at all? "Although tares are seen to be in the Church," he says. He says "are seen," not "are believed on suspicion." The Latin word can also mean "seem," so someone might think he meant that they only seemed to be there and were not really there. To rule this out, he makes his meaning clear in the words that follow: "this ought not to hinder our faith or our love, so that we ourselves withdraw from the Church because we see that there are tares in it." He does not say "we suspect, we think, we believe, we suppose," but "we see." The servants who said to the householder, "Do you want us to go and gather them up?" were not believing in things concealed, but seeing things in plain view. Of these tares it had been said, "When the blade had sprung up and borne fruit, then the tares appeared." He answered them, "No, lest in gathering the tares you root up the wheat along with them," and, "Let both grow until the harvest." And yet you say that only tares have grown throughout the world and that the wheat has dwindled and perished in almost the whole world. In saying this, what are you doing but contradicting the Lord? The Church has not yet reached some nations in its growth. But it must reach them: the gospel must be preached in the whole world, and then the end will come. The Lord foretold this without any ambiguity.

You see that, on Cyprian's testimony, the Church is called catholic from "the whole," and is not without manifest wicked people, though he warns that it must not be abandoned on their account. There are many good people in it, considered in themselves, but they are certainly few compared with the tares or the chaff. What the Lord himself says comes about not outside the Church but within it: "Because iniquity has abounded, the love of many will grow cold." But within it too is the people spread everywhere, to whom it is said: "Whoever perseveres to the end will be saved." Those, however, who have faith like a grain of mustard seed, faith that can move even mountains, are very rare indeed. It was of that kind of faith that the Lord said, "When the Son of Man comes, do you think he will find faith on earth?" He was not speaking of the apostasy of the whole world, as you most perversely understand it.

Now about baptism. You think it does not exist except in the Church, and so you criticize us because we hold that those who come from heresies, if they have already been baptized, should not be baptized again. Here it is enough to point out that you were quite unable to answer one question: how could Felicianus baptize, when he had been condemned and placed outside your church? You tried in vain to count him among those to whom you granted a delay. Read the sentence of your council of Bagai. After the many very harsh things it says against them, things far more serious than were said against Caecilian when your forebears condemned him in his absence and in his innocence, it adds their manifest and undoubted condemnation in these words: "Know, therefore, that these men, guilty of a notorious crime, have been condemned by the judgment of God presiding, through the truthful mouth of the universal council: Victorianus of Carcabia, Marcianus of Sullecthum, Beianus of Beia, Salvius of Ausafa, Theodorus of Usula, Donatus of Sabratha, Miggin of Elefantaria, Praetextatus of Assuras, Salvius of Membresa, Valerius of Melzi, Felicianus of Musti and Martialis of Pertusa, who by a deadly work of perdition glued together a filthy vessel out of collected dregs; and also the clergy who once belonged to the church of Carthage, who by taking part in this crime acted as procurers for an unlawful incest." Then it begins to grant a delay to the rest, in these words: "But those whose seedlings were not defiled by the sacrilegious shoot, that is, those who out of the modest shame of faith drew back their hands from Maximian's head, we have permitted to return to mother church." I have already said enough about these men in my earlier letter to you. Anyone who reads it and pays a little attention cannot doubt that you were completely unable to answer this point.

So it is pointless for you to think that the councils of Agrippinus and Cyprian should be followed on this question. You yourselves ignored them when you received people who had been baptized outside your communion by men you had condemned, and you did not repeat their baptism, even though you had gone to law against those men to have them shut out of the basilicas. As for the opinion of Cyprian and his colleagues, who held at that time that those coming from heretics ought to be baptized, it would take a long time to discuss it as it deserves. But solve this short question for me, if you can. When Cyprian, bishop of the church of Carthage, was rebaptizing those who came from heretics, Stephen, bishop of the church of Rome, was at that same time receiving heretics with the baptism they had received outside. Though they did these different things, both remained in catholic unity. Through Stephen and his countless colleagues throughout the world who shared his view, the Church was then, according to you, receiving people guilty of every crime without baptism. Tell me whether at that time the Church perished through contact with the wicked or not. You cannot say that these wicked people were hidden, though you claim that even hidden wicked people do harm and bring death. Consider anyone baptized among heretics who came to Stephen and his associates: a murderer, even a parricide, an adulterer, someone guilty of incest, an idolater, or finally a traditor who handed over the holy books without even the excuse of fear, or who cruelly tortured and violently forced others to hand them over, and then burned them himself or ordered them burned. According to you, such a person was received without baptism. So you see that, if your view of baptism is true, all the crimes of mankind were at that time gathered into the Church without baptism. Answer whether Cyprian was stained by these crimes within that same unity. Answer whether the Church perished or not. Choose whichever you think. If it had already perished then, who gave birth to Donatus? But if it could not perish even when so many were joined to it without baptism, then answer, I beg you: what madness persuaded the party of Donatus to separate from it, as if to avoid communion with the wicked?

Blessed Cyprian held a view on baptism different from the one the truth has shown, first through custom and later through reasoning examined more carefully. But God forbid that any of us, because we understand what he did not, should dare on that account to set himself above him. His many other great merits, his spirit filled with outstanding love, which kept him wholly at peace with colleagues who held a different view, and his glorious martyrdom in the unity of the Church have shown clearly enough that he was a fruitful branch on the root of Christ. The Father would prune this branch even of this fault, so that it could bear more fruit. For Jesus himself says, "Every branch in me that bears fruit, my Father prunes, so that it may bear more fruit." He shows that even in fruitful branches the vinedresser who is in heaven finds something to prune. Which of us can be compared with the apostle Peter, even though we have never compelled Gentiles to live like Jews, as he was doing when he was not walking straight according to the truth of the gospel? He was corrected by the wholesome admonition of Paul, who became an apostle after him, and so he left later generations a more useful example of humility than if there had been nothing in him to correct.

We stand, then, in this Church, which could not and cannot perish through contact with wicked people, whether hidden or manifest. So we fear no slanders about anyone at all. If such people are wicked, then either the good certainly do not know them; or, once the wicked have been exposed by evidence against them, the good condemn them under the laws of the Church; or, if the good know them but cannot condemn them because they have not been accused and convicted before them, they tolerate them for the sake of the Church's peace. In doing so they are not only blameless but praiseworthy. They do not tear the Lord's nets and damnably separate themselves because of the bad fish before the time of the shore. If they wanted to do so, they are forbidden by countless testimonies of the divine Scriptures. But leaving those aside, they are certainly held back by the most blessed Cyprian, the very witness you brought forward. He cries out and solemnly declares that "although tares are seen to be in the Church, this ought not to hinder our faith or our love, so that we ourselves withdraw from the Church because we see that there are tares in it." He teaches us this not only by his words but also by his own example. He had colleagues who seized estates by treacherous frauds and swelled their profits with compound interest, and he understood their greed, following the apostle, to be no slight fault but idolatry. Yet he bore with such men for the sake of the bond of unity, and he did not become like them through contact with them. He departed from them by being unlike them in conduct, not by dividing the sacraments. He did not touch the unclean thing, but he avoided it by shrinking from their deeds, not by gathering a separate people. But you understand carnally what was said through the prophet Isaiah: "Depart, come out from among them and be separate, says the Lord, and touch nothing unclean," along with other similar sayings in the Scriptures. As long as you understand these things carnally rather than spiritually, you show yourselves to be exactly like the people whom that same prophet condemns, those who say, "Do not touch me, for I am clean." In short, while you perversely decided that other people's sins must be avoided, you committed sins of your own. You divided peoples in a sacrilegious schism, and with a wicked spirit you held a sacrilegious heresy about the Church spread throughout the whole world, against the plain promises of God, which have been fulfilled. You think, and you criticize our wording on this point, that one and the same society of the lost cannot be both a schism and a heresy at once. If that were so, the most blessed Cyprian would not have said what he did in this very letter, from which I took the testimony about the tares in the Church. Writing to the confessors whom he congratulated on being set free from the Novatianist division, he said: "I grieved deeply and was sorely distressed that I could not be in communion with those whom I had once begun to love, after a schismatic and heretical error took hold of you as you came out of prison." So do not fly in the face of the plainest truth by deceitfully dodging both charges, or by choosing whichever of the two seems milder to you. For you are both a schismatic, by your sacrilegious departure, and a heretic, by your sacrilegious doctrine.

And do not flatter yourselves that we do not annul your baptism. It is not yours. It belongs to the Catholic Church, which we hold, and when you left her you took it with you, not for your salvation but for your ruin. Even the Lord's vessels remained holy among foreigners. The king who dared to treat them with contempt was punished by an angry God, and the ark of the covenant, though captured by enemies, in no way lost the power of its holiness. Those holy things were among strangers in such a way that they ceased to be among their own people, and yet they could not lose the force of their holiness at all. How much less, then, do the Christian sacraments lose it, when they pass over to heretics in such a way that they also remain with us! This is what I said when I wrote to you. We also said it to you at the conference, and you thought it better to evade it, because you could not refute it. The apostle says of certain people that they "hold the truth in iniquity"; in the same way you hold the truth of divine baptism in the iniquity of human error. That truth is not yours, and we certainly ought not to annul it because of your iniquity. Since the apostle is understood to have said "who hold the truth in iniquity" of the idolatrous Gentiles, you demanded of me, as though in reply, that I prove what part of the Gentiles' sacrilege the apostle does not annul, what part of their profane rites he does not condemn. As if he could fail to annul and condemn what is sacrilegious and profane, just as we condemn your schism and your heresy! Yet there are certain true statements about the unknown God held by some of the Gentile philosophers, and the apostle not only did not destroy them but even cited them as testimony when there was need. Speaking to the Athenians about God, he says: "For in him we live and move and have our being, as even some of your own have said." The blessed Paul not only did not destroy this truth of wisdom but actually used it to instruct them, while they held it in the iniquity of their idolatry, which the apostle's teaching overthrew by apostolic means. In the same way, the true things that your forebears received in the Catholic Church and handed down to you we do not annul but acknowledge. Your sacrilege, however, we either annul when you are converted or abhor while you persist.

And yet you have settled the whole question, everything at issue between us, by your careful explanation of a single word of the tribune's. I had said: "Nor do we read in the tribune's letter that the name of God was invoked by you in truth," because I had not found that very word there at all. You replied: "You are mistaken, or rather you are deceiving. For the tribune's words are: 'lest so great a work, the house of the Lord, where the name of God and of his Christ has often been invoked by you, be said to have been burned by Your Religiousness, residing there.' Understand that 'religion' is said of what is in truth, while what is in falsehood is called 'superstition.'" When would I have noticed that, when would I have reasoned that way, when would I have proved one thing from another like that? I confess it escaped the sharpness of my wits, such as they are. So believe me that I could have been mistaken there, and did not, as you said, mean to deceive over a word. The tribune, then, being a military man, made a mistake when he said "Your Religiousness" to someone he knows or believes to be a heretic, since heresy is not religion but superstition, and in proper usage religion is spoken of not in falsehood but in truth. So by this explanation of yours, the true worship of God is called religion and false worship is called superstition. Listen, then, to yourself; heed your own words, and you will not at all refuse to follow us. For when you wrote to that same tribune, at the very opening of your first letter, you put this: "To the honorable Dulcitius, tribune and notary, much to be longed for by us if you so wish, Gaudentius the bishop," and you went straight on: "I have received the letter of Your Religiousness." Why then do you still hesitate to come over to us? Look: the tribune Dulcitius is a man of our communion, and yet by your own testimony he is not superstitious but religious. So by your explanation he holds not a false worship of God but the true one. He, then, is in the Catholic Church rather than you, since you were so far from mistaken about this word that you even explained that religion differs from superstition as much as truth differs from falsehood. That man, as I said, is a soldier, not well trained in these niceties of language, and he did not know what religion meant. Far be it from me to say that he was deceiving you with flattery. But you refute your opponents with the words of the prophet and cry out: "Woe to those who call bitter sweet and sweet bitter, who call light darkness and darkness light." If what Dulcitius holds with us is superstition, why did you call it religion? And if you spoke the truth, why do you cling to heretical superstition and spurn Catholic religion? Follow your own testimony, then, especially since your own people, once they learn of it, may well refuse communion with you, because by this word you have entered into communion with the tribune Dulcitius. Come now, brother Gaudentius, do not lose the opportunity the Lord has given you, even through your own tongue. Or are you perhaps angry that I call you brother? For you rejected this name from us even at our conference, and there you showed that we are those whom the Lord commanded through the prophet, "Say, 'You are our brothers,' to those who hate you and detest you," while you are among those who hate and detest the ones to whom the Lord says this. You certainly cannot deny that you called the faith to which the tribune Dulcitius belongs a religion. That is why he sent you that letter: so that you would not kill yourself, and so that you would enter into communion with the church to which he belongs. If, then, his is religion, yours is superstition. Each of you has said this to the other, yet you choose to have him be the one who spoke falsely rather than yourself.

Therefore, by this most true testimony of yours and your most true explanation, since what the tribune Dulcitius holds is religion, then it is surely religion by which the emperor's command is urging you into our communion. It follows that it is also religion by which a Christian emperor judges that it belongs to his care to see that offenses against divine things do not go unpunished, although you would have him care only for what is contained in the earthly commonwealth. That is why, forgetting what you have read, you said that the king of the Ninevites did not command the people to do penance. These are your words to me: "Why," you say, "do you deceive the wretched? God gave the command to Jonah; the Lord sent the prophet to the people; he commanded nothing of the sort to the king." Pay attention, then, to what is written, and be angry with no one but yourself, since either you do not remember the divine Scriptures or it is rather you who deceive the wretched: "Jonah arose and went to Nineveh, as the Lord had spoken. Now Nineveh was a great city, about three days' journey across. And Jonah began to go into the city about one day's journey, and he preached and said, 'Yet three days, and Nineveh shall be overthrown.' And the men of Nineveh believed the Lord, and they proclaimed a fast and put on sackcloth, from the greatest to the least. When word reached the king of the city of Nineveh, he rose from his throne, took off his robes, covered himself with sackcloth, and sat down in ashes. And it was proclaimed by the king and his nobles, saying: 'Let neither man nor beast, sheep nor ox, taste anything or graze, and let them not drink water.' And men and beasts were clothed in sackcloth; they cried earnestly to the Lord, and each one turned from his evil way and from the iniquity that was in his hands." Do you hear at last that the king concerned himself with what you are displeased to see as belonging to the care of kings? Certainly he did so in order that what was being done less than it ought to have been might be done earnestly. The reason the Ninevites were not driven to penance by the king's authority through confiscations and proscriptions or the terror of soldiers is that they obediently did what they were told. So we do not show the people suffering such things, because you cannot show that the king was defied either. Accordingly, whoever obeys kings when, in religious fear, they command what accords with God, beginning from fear and advancing to love, receives peace from the Lord, not as the world gives peace. For the world gives peace for the sake of temporal advantage, but the Lord for the sake of eternal salvation. So, since the faith to which the tribune Dulcitius belongs is religion (and you are not going to deny your own words), the party of Donatus, from which his religion wants to rescue you, is superstition. It is superstition that you seek to kill yourself, which his religion strictly forbids. It is superstition that you find fault with the emperor's concern over these matters, a concern which his religion has undertaken to carry out.

So, since the case has been closed by your own word, I implore you by the God of religion, the God of truth, that your error too may at last be closed. This, brother, is the church of Christ, which in this present time is spreading and growing throughout the whole world, holding both bad and good, who are to be separated at the final winnowing. And to address you, in closing, rather in the words of the man you chose to call as a witness to the Catholic name: she it is who, flooded with the Lord's light, sends forth her rays through the whole world; she it is who stretches out her branches over all the earth in abundant fruitfulness. Therefore, "even if there seem to be tares in her, our faith or our love ought not to be hindered, so that, because we see that there are tares in the church, we ourselves withdraw from the church. We must only labor to be wheat, so that when the wheat begins to be gathered into the Lord's barns, we may receive the fruit of our work and labor. The apostle says in his epistle: 'In a great house there are not only vessels of gold and silver but also of wood and earthenware, some for honor and some for dishonor.' Let us strive and labor as much as we can to be a vessel of gold or silver. But to break the earthen vessels is granted to the Lord alone, to whom the rod of iron has also been given. The servant cannot be greater than his master, nor should anyone claim for himself what the Father has granted to the Son alone, so as to think that he can already carry the fan or winnowing shovel to winnow and cleanse the threshing floor, or separate all the tares from the wheat by human judgment. That is proud obstinacy and sacrilegious presumption, which depraved madness takes upon itself. And while some always take upon themselves more than gentle justice demands, they perish from the church; and while they insolently exalt themselves, blinded by their own swelling pride, they lose the light of truth." These are the words of the most blessed Cyprian, not mine: the words, that is, of the man whom you set at the opening of your writings as a most select witness to the Catholic name for us, and whom you commended at great length on many points. Indeed, since they are true and divine, they are words of God spoken through him. Hear this, then; beware of this, so that, with the help of the Savior's mercy, we may together hold Catholic charity, together love Catholic peace, together grow everywhere with its wheat, together bear with the tares until the end, and together live without end in the barn. You surely see that, without any defense of Caecilian or of any other men whom you think should be accused, the Catholic Church stands firm in her own strength and solidity. And yet our conference did clear Caecilian's case, and as for the others you slander, either the charge is doubtful or the condemnation unjust. But it is utterly foolish, with reasoning gone astray, to stake the church's cause, supported and fortified by divine testimonies, on the cases of men. For even if we saw quite plainly that those men were bad and could no longer separate them from the church's sacraments, still our faith or our love ought not to be hindered, so that, because we saw them too among the tares in the church, we should ourselves withdraw from the church. If you are thinking of replying, do not abandon the issue and wander off into irrelevancies. Look at what has been said, and answer what has been said, not by evading it deceitfully but by arguing reasonably. As for what you accomplished in that long-winded reply of yours, or rather how completely you accomplished nothing, I will demonstrate that more carefully in another work, if it seems necessary and the Lord grants it.
Against Gaudentius, Bishop of the Donatists: Two Books.

At about the same time Dulcitius, tribune and notary, was here in Africa carrying out the imperial orders issued against the Donatists. He had sent a letter to Gaudentius of Thamugadi, a bishop of the Donatists and one of the seven they had chosen to plead their case at our conference. In it he urged him toward catholic unity and tried to dissuade him from the fire with which he was threatening to burn himself and his people, together with the very church he was in. He added that, if they thought themselves righteous, they should rather flee, as the Lord Christ commanded, than burn themselves in unspeakable flames. Gaudentius wrote two letters in reply: one short, because, as he claimed, the messenger was in a hurry, and another long one, as though he were answering more fully and carefully. The tribune I have mentioned thought these should be sent to me so that I could refute them myself instead. I answered both of them in one book. When this came into Gaudentius's hands, he wrote back to me whatever he saw fit, answering with no reasoning at all, but rather showing that he could neither answer nor keep silent. Although this would be clear enough to those who read intelligently and compare our words with his, I still did not wish to leave whatever it was without a reply. That is how these two books of mine against him came about.
This work begins thus: "Gaudentius, the Donatist bishop of Thamugadi."
The Surviving Decisions of the Council of Bagai, Collected from Various Passages of Augustine.

By the will of almighty God and of his Christ, our Saviour, we came from all the provinces of Africa and held a council in the holy church of Bagai: Gamalius, Primian, Pontius, Secundianus, Januarianus, Saturninus, Felix, Pegasius, Rufinus, Fortunius, Crispinus, Florentius, Optatus, Donatus, Donatian and the rest, three hundred and ten in number. It seemed good to the Holy Spirit who is in us to establish lasting peace and to cut off sacrilegious schisms ...

.... The longed-for brotherhood of peace and concord has indeed been joined together, as it is written: "Righteousness and peace have kissed each other." But the shipwrecked limbs of some have been hurled by the wave of truth onto jagged rocks. Just like the Egyptians who perished, the shores are full of their corpses, and for them the punishment is greater in death itself, because after the avenging waters have wrung out their life, they cannot even find a burial ....

.... For although the channel of a poisoned womb long concealed the harmful offspring of the viper's seed, and the moist clots of conceived crime were slowly warmed into the limbs of asps, still the venom once conceived could not be hidden under a vanishing shade. For though late, their wishes, pregnant with crimes, have given birth to their public outrage and their parricide, as was foretold long ago: "He was in labour with injustice, he conceived sorrow and brought forth iniquity." But now that clear sky shines out from the cloud and the forest of crimes is no longer a tangle, since the names have been marked out for punishment (for until now there had been indulgence), as we let go the line of clemency, the case has found those whom it should punish .....

.... Let us speak, dearest brothers, of the causes of the schism, since we can no longer keep silent about the persons. Maximian, rival of the faith, adulterer of the truth, enemy of mother church, servant of Dathan, Korah and Abiram, has been struck from the bosom of peace by the thunderbolt of our sentence. And that the earth has not yet opened and swallowed him up means only that he has been kept among those above ground for a greater punishment. Had he been snatched away, he would have gained his punishment by the shortcut of death; now he is collecting the interest of a heavier debt, since he is dead and yet lives among the living.

Nor is he the only one whom a just death condemns for his crime; the chain of sacrilege also drags very many into partnership in his guilt, of whom it is written: "The poison of asps is under their lips; their mouth is full of cursing and bitterness. Their feet are swift to shed blood. Ruin and misery are in their ways, and the way of peace they have not known. There is no fear of God before their eyes." We would not, indeed, have wished them to be cut away as though from a joint of our own body. But since the pestilent rot of a festering wound finds more relief in amputation than in the leniency of medicine, a healthier course has been found: so that the pestilent poison does not creep through all the limbs, the wound that has arisen should be cut away at the cost of a brief pain.

Know, therefore, that those guilty of a notorious crime have been condemned by the truthful voice of the universal council, at the judgment of God who presides over it: Victorianus of Carcabia, Marcianus of Sullecti, Beianus of Beia, Salvius of Ausafa, Theodorus of Usula, Donatus of Sabratha, Miggin of Elefantaria, Praetextatus of Assuras, Salvius of Membressa, Valerius of Melzi, Felicianus of Musti and Martialis of Pertusa, who by their deadly work of perdition gathered up the dregs and glued together a filthy vessel; and also the clergy formerly of the church of Carthage, who by taking part in the crime acted as procurers for that unlawful incest. But those whose young shoots the sacrilegious cuttings did not defile, that is, those who out of the reverent modesty of faith held back their hands from the head of Maximian, we have permitted to return to mother church.

For the more we are cleansed by the death of the guilty, the more we rejoice at the return of the innocent. And so that a short time, under the pressure of a tight deadline, does not take away the hope of salvation from those returning, we open the door of acknowledgment to all who are allowed to acknowledge, while the previous decrees remain in force, until the eighth day before the Kalends of January next, so that those who return may keep the foundations of their honour and faith undiminished. If anyone through sluggish idleness fails to enter it, let him know that by his own will he has cut himself off from every way to pardon. For the sentence pronounced will remain upon them, and for those who return after the appointed day a fixed penance .......
